title: Depth-nonuniform LoRA rank allocation for SAM
one_line_idea: Allocate LoRA rank nonuniformly across SAM encoder depth based on where the target domain gap concentrates, instead of the uniform-rank default.
problem: SAM LoRA recipes assign the same rank to every transformer block even though domain shift plausibly stresses different depths differently.
core_hypothesis: For texture-level shifts (e.g., medical grayscale imagery) most useful adaptation lives in early blocks, so shifting rank budget toward early layers beats uniform allocation at equal parameter count.
falsifiable_prediction: At matched total adapter parameters, an early-heavy rank profile outperforms uniform rank on texture-shifted targets, and the advantage disappears or reverses on shape-shifted targets.
why_important: A placement rule that depends on shift type would turn PEFT configuration from folklore into a diagnostic-driven procedure and save tuning compute for every downstream SAM user.
why_possibly_novel: Nonuniform rank allocation exists for LLMs, but a shift-type-conditioned allocation rule for promptable segmentation encoders is not something I can point to as established; novelty unverified.
minimal_falsification_experiment: Take one texture-shifted and one shape-shifted segmentation dataset; train uniform, early-heavy, and late-heavy rank profiles at identical parameter budgets and compare Dice/boundary-F1 with 3 seeds.
main_risk: Optimizer dynamics may equalize what each profile learns, making all allocations statistically indistinguishable at practical budgets.
community_default_belief: Uniform LoRA rank across all blocks is good enough and rank placement is a second-order detail.
why_it_might_be_wrong: Uniformity is a convenience default inherited from NLP; dense prediction has strong depth-specific feature roles (edges early, semantics late) that plausibly break it.
fastest_falsifying_experiment: One dataset, rank budget fixed, three allocation profiles, 1-epoch training each; if curves are already indistinguishable the effect is likely too weak to matter.
core_claim: For texture-level shifts (e.g., medical grayscale imagery) most useful adaptation lives in early blocks, so shifting rank budget toward early layers beats uniform allocation at equal parameter count.
method_sketch: Take one texture-shifted and one shape-shifted segmentation dataset; train uniform, early-heavy, and late-heavy rank profiles at identical parameter budgets and compare Dice/boundary-F1 with 3 seeds.
novelty_hook: Nonuniform rank allocation exists for LLMs, but a shift-type-conditioned allocation rule for promptable segmentation encoders is not something I can point to as established; novelty unverified.
kill_risk: Optimizer dynamics may equalize what each profile learns, making all allocations statistically indistinguishable at practical budgets.

title: Attention-LoRA vs MLP-LoRA dichotomy in SAM
one_line_idea: Test whether MLP-only LoRA adapts SAM to texture-shifted domains while attention-only LoRA is what shape/grouping-shifted domains need.
problem: Practitioners place LoRA on QKV projections by default without evidence that attention is where segmentation domain gaps live.
core_hypothesis: MLP adapters absorb appearance/texture statistics while attention adapters change token grouping, so the winning placement is predictable from the type of domain shift.
falsifiable_prediction: MLP-only LoRA beats attention-only LoRA at equal budget on appearance-shifted data, and the ordering flips on datasets whose objects require new grouping (e.g., thin elongated structures).
why_important: It would give the first mechanistic placement rule for segmentation PEFT and halve adapter size for many deployments.
why_possibly_novel: Placement ablations exist in scattered papers, but a shift-type-conditional theory of attention-vs-MLP placement for promptable segmentation is, to my knowledge, unarticulated; novelty unverified.
minimal_falsification_experiment: Two datasets chosen to differ in shift type; train attention-only, MLP-only, and both-placements LoRA at matched parameters; compare masks plus attention-map drift analysis.
main_risk: Shift types are rarely pure, so real datasets may mix both and blur the predicted dichotomy.
community_default_belief: QKV LoRA placement transfers from LLM practice to vision encoders essentially unchanged.
why_it_might_be_wrong: Segmentation quality depends on spatial grouping structure that language-model-derived placement folklore never had to model.
fastest_falsifying_experiment: Single texture-shifted dataset: if attention-only matches MLP-only there within a seed's noise after short training, the dichotomy is likely false.
core_claim: MLP adapters absorb appearance/texture statistics while attention adapters change token grouping, so the winning placement is predictable from the type of domain shift.
method_sketch: Two datasets chosen to differ in shift type; train attention-only, MLP-only, and both-placements LoRA at matched parameters; compare masks plus attention-map drift analysis.
novelty_hook: Placement ablations exist in scattered papers, but a shift-type-conditional theory of attention-vs-MLP placement for promptable segmentation is, to my knowledge, unarticulated; novelty unverified.
kill_risk: Shift types are rarely pure, so real datasets may mix both and blur the predicted dichotomy.

title: Decoder-only tuning as a sufficiency baseline
one_line_idea: Claim that for a large fraction of reported SAM adaptation wins, tuning only the lightweight mask decoder reproduces most of the gain attributed to encoder-side PEFT.
problem: Encoder LoRA is treated as necessary, but the mask decoder is tiny and cheap to tune, and few works report a serious decoder-only baseline.
core_hypothesis: SAM's frozen encoder features are already sufficient for many target domains and most adaptation gain is decoder re-reading of those features.
falsifiable_prediction: Decoder-only fine-tuning reaches within a small margin of encoder-LoRA Dice on several appearance-shifted benchmarks at a fraction of trainable parameters.
why_important: If true, much published complexity is unnecessary and deployment becomes trivially cheap; if false, we learn encoder features genuinely lack target information.
why_possibly_novel: Decoder-only tuning appears as an occasional ablation, but positioning it as a systematic sufficiency test across shift types seems underexplored; novelty unverified.
minimal_falsification_experiment: On three domains of increasing shift severity, compare decoder-only tuning vs encoder LoRA vs both, at matched training steps, reporting Dice and boundary metrics.
main_risk: Severe modality shifts (e.g., non-RGB physics) likely need encoder change, limiting the claim's scope to moderate shifts.
community_default_belief: The encoder must be adapted because domain shift corrupts its features.
why_it_might_be_wrong: Feature corruption may be superficial: information may survive linearly readable in frozen features, needing only a new reader.
fastest_falsifying_experiment: Linear-probe frozen encoder features for target masks; if probing is near-random the sufficiency claim dies immediately.
core_claim: SAM's frozen encoder features are already sufficient for many target domains and most adaptation gain is decoder re-reading of those features.
method_sketch: On three domains of increasing shift severity, compare decoder-only tuning vs encoder LoRA vs both, at matched training steps, reporting Dice and boundary metrics.
novelty_hook: Decoder-only tuning appears as an occasional ablation, but positioning it as a systematic sufficiency test across shift types seems underexplored; novelty unverified.
kill_risk: Severe modality shifts (e.g., non-RGB physics) likely need encoder change, limiting the claim's scope to moderate shifts.

title: Value-projection-only LoRA preserves promptability
one_line_idea: Adapt only the V (value) projections in SAM attention, hypothesizing Q/K adaptation is what damages interactive prompt behavior.
problem: Full QKV adaptation changes where attention looks, which may silently break the click-to-mask geometry SAM was pretrained to honor.
core_hypothesis: Domain adaptation mostly requires re-describing content (V) rather than re-routing attention (Q/K), so V-only LoRA gets comparable target gains with less zero-shot and promptability degradation.
falsifiable_prediction: V-only LoRA matches QKV LoRA target Dice within noise while showing measurably smaller degradation on held-out generic interactive segmentation.
why_important: A placement that decouples domain gain from promptability loss would make adapted SAMs safer to reuse as general interactive tools.
why_possibly_novel: Projection-wise asymmetry studies exist for LLMs, but tying V-only placement to preserved interactive promptability in segmentation is a specific unverified twist.
minimal_falsification_experiment: Train V-only, QK-only, and QKV LoRA on one medical dataset; evaluate target Dice plus a fixed suite of zero-shot click-prompt tests on natural images.
main_risk: Attention re-routing may be exactly what hard domains require, making V-only strictly weaker where it matters most.
community_default_belief: Adapting all of QKV is the safe default and promptability degradation is negligible or unmeasured.
why_it_might_be_wrong: Nobody routinely measures interactive degradation, so the community may simply not see the damage QK adaptation causes.
fastest_falsifying_experiment: After one short QKV-LoRA run, replay a fixed set of click prompts on out-of-domain images and quantify mask drift vs the frozen model; if drift is tiny the motivation collapses.
core_claim: Domain adaptation mostly requires re-describing content (V) rather than re-routing attention (Q/K), so V-only LoRA gets comparable target gains with less zero-shot and promptability degradation.
method_sketch: Train V-only, QK-only, and QKV LoRA on one medical dataset; evaluate target Dice plus a fixed suite of zero-shot click-prompt tests on natural images.
novelty_hook: Projection-wise asymmetry studies exist for LLMs, but tying V-only placement to preserved interactive promptability in segmentation is a specific unverified twist.
kill_risk: Attention re-routing may be exactly what hard domains require, making V-only strictly weaker where it matters most.

title: One-epoch saliency probe for layer-selective LoRA
one_line_idea: Use a single cheap probe epoch measuring per-layer gradient saliency to choose the top-k SAM layers for LoRA, matching all-layer adaptation at a fraction of the parameters.
problem: Layer selection for adapters is done by grid search or not at all, wasting compute and parameters.
core_hypothesis: Early gradient-norm or Fisher-style saliency per layer is a reliable predictor of where adaptation capacity is needed for a given target dataset.
falsifiable_prediction: Top-25% saliency-selected layers achieve at least 95% of all-layer LoRA's Dice gain across multiple targets, beating random and uniform-spread selections of the same size.
why_important: Turns adapter placement into an automatic, dataset-conditioned procedure and cuts adapter memory for multi-domain serving.
why_possibly_novel: Saliency-guided placement has analogues in pruning literature; applying it as a pre-training-step selector for segmentation PEFT is plausibly underexplored; unverified.
minimal_falsification_experiment: On three datasets, rank layers by probe saliency, train LoRA on top-k vs random-k vs bottom-k, and test whether saliency ordering predicts final performance ordering.
main_risk: Early-training saliency may reflect loss-surface curvature quirks rather than where durable adaptation ends up living.
community_default_belief: Where you put adapters matters less than total capacity, so uniform placement is fine.
why_it_might_be_wrong: Matched-capacity comparisons across placements are rarely run, so the belief rests on absence of evidence.
fastest_falsifying_experiment: Correlate probe saliency with per-layer LoRA-norm after a full training run on one dataset; near-zero correlation kills the predictor.
core_claim: Early gradient-norm or Fisher-style saliency per layer is a reliable predictor of where adaptation capacity is needed for a given target dataset.
method_sketch: On three datasets, rank layers by probe saliency, train LoRA on top-k vs random-k vs bottom-k, and test whether saliency ordering predicts final performance ordering.
novelty_hook: Saliency-guided placement has analogues in pruning literature; applying it as a pre-training-step selector for segmentation PEFT is plausibly underexplored; unverified.
kill_risk: Early-training saliency may reflect loss-surface curvature quirks rather than where durable adaptation ends up living.

title: BitFit-style bias-only tuning as an unbeaten baseline
one_line_idea: Systematically test whether bias-only tuning of SAM, an almost-free baseline, matches published adapter methods at their own evaluation protocols.
problem: SAM adaptation papers compare against full fine-tuning and each other but rarely against the cheapest credible baseline, bias-only tuning.
core_hypothesis: A nontrivial fraction of reported SAM-adapter gains are reproducible with bias terms alone, implying those methods mostly re-scale features.
falsifiable_prediction: Bias-only tuning lands within a small Dice margin of at least some adapter-based recipes on moderate-shift targets at orders of magnitude fewer trainable parameters.
why_important: Establishes the true baseline floor for the subfield and deflates methods whose gains come from any trainable capacity at all.
why_possibly_novel: Bias-only tuning is known in NLP; using it as an adversarial audit baseline for the SAM adaptation literature seems not systematically done; unverified.
minimal_falsification_experiment: Reimplement a common evaluation setup on two or three public segmentation targets, run bias-only vs LoRA vs adapter layers under identical schedules, and report the gap distribution.
main_risk: Bias-only may genuinely collapse on large shifts, making the audit unremarkable where adapters are actually needed.
community_default_belief: Adapter architectures contribute method-specific value beyond generic trainable capacity.
why_it_might_be_wrong: Matched-budget-and-schedule audits are rare, and simple capacity effects have repeatedly explained away architecture claims in other subfields.
fastest_falsifying_experiment: One target dataset, one afternoon: bias-only vs one popular adapter recipe at the same schedule; a large persistent gap weakens the audit's premise.
core_claim: A nontrivial fraction of reported SAM-adapter gains are reproducible with bias terms alone, implying those methods mostly re-scale features.
method_sketch: Reimplement a common evaluation setup on two or three public segmentation targets, run bias-only vs LoRA vs adapter layers under identical schedules, and report the gap distribution.
novelty_hook: Bias-only tuning is known in NLP; using it as an adversarial audit baseline for the SAM adaptation literature seems not systematically done; unverified.
kill_risk: Bias-only may genuinely collapse on large shifts, making the audit unremarkable where adapters are actually needed.

title: Positional-embedding-only adaptation for scale-shifted imagery
one_line_idea: For scale/resolution-shifted domains such as aerial or microscopy imagery, adapt only SAM's positional embeddings and neck while freezing everything else.
problem: Ground-sample-distance and magnification shifts change object scale statistics, which SAM encodes partly in positional structure, yet PEFT recipes ignore this locus.
core_hypothesis: A large share of scale-shift adaptation is achievable by retuning positional embeddings plus the convolutional neck, without touching transformer weights.
falsifiable_prediction: Pos-embed+neck tuning recovers a majority of the gap between frozen SAM and full LoRA on scale-shifted targets while failing to do so on pure appearance-shifted targets.
why_important: Identifies a physically interpretable, extremely small adaptation locus for a whole family of domains (remote sensing, microscopy).
why_possibly_novel: Resolution interpolation of pos-embeds is standard practice; treating pos-embed tuning as the primary PEFT mechanism for scale shift appears untested as a hypothesis; unverified.
minimal_falsification_experiment: On one aerial and one microscopy dataset vs one texture-shifted control, compare frozen, pos-embed+neck, LoRA, and combined variants at matched schedules.
main_risk: Scale statistics may be absorbed throughout attention layers, leaving pos-embeds a minor lever.
community_default_belief: Positional embeddings are a preprocessing detail to interpolate, not a meaningful adaptation target.
why_it_might_be_wrong: Window-attention ViTs encode scale-sensitive inductive structure in position handling, so the 'detail' may carry real domain content.
fastest_falsifying_experiment: Freeze all but pos-embeds on one aerial dataset for a short run; if the loss barely moves relative to a frozen baseline, the locus is too weak.
core_claim: A large share of scale-shift adaptation is achievable by retuning positional embeddings plus the convolutional neck, without touching transformer weights.
method_sketch: On one aerial and one microscopy dataset vs one texture-shifted control, compare frozen, pos-embed+neck, LoRA, and combined variants at matched schedules.
novelty_hook: Resolution interpolation of pos-embeds is standard practice; treating pos-embed tuning as the primary PEFT mechanism for scale shift appears untested as a hypothesis; unverified.
kill_risk: Scale statistics may be absorbed throughout attention layers, leaving pos-embeds a minor lever.

title: Neck-only convolutional LoRA for dense adaptation
one_line_idea: Place low-rank adapters only in SAM's convolutional neck (the encoder-to-embedding projection) rather than in transformer blocks.
problem: The neck is where 2D spatial structure is re-imposed on ViT tokens, a natural bottleneck for dense-task adaptation that PEFT literature bypasses.
core_hypothesis: Adapting the neck reshapes the spatial feature map enough to fix many boundary-quality failures at near-zero parameter cost.
falsifiable_prediction: Neck-only adaptation improves boundary-F1 substantially more than region Dice, and captures a disproportionate share of full-LoRA boundary gains.
why_important: A boundary-targeted micro-adapter would serve applications (medical, matting-adjacent) where boundary quality, not region overlap, is the deliverable.
why_possibly_novel: Most SAM PEFT targets transformer internals; deliberate neck-only adaptation with boundary-metric analysis seems unexplored; unverified.
minimal_falsification_experiment: Train neck-only vs block-LoRA on two boundary-sensitive datasets; decompose gains into trimap boundary vs interior regions.
main_risk: The neck's capacity may be too small to express needed corrections, capping gains at trivial levels.
community_default_belief: Meaningful adaptation requires touching the transformer blocks where representation power lives.
why_it_might_be_wrong: Dense-prediction failures are often re-projection failures rather than representation failures, and the neck is exactly the re-projection.
fastest_falsifying_experiment: Short neck-only run on one dataset with trimap evaluation; no boundary-specific advantage over frozen baseline kills the hypothesis.
core_claim: Adapting the neck reshapes the spatial feature map enough to fix many boundary-quality failures at near-zero parameter cost.
method_sketch: Train neck-only vs block-LoRA on two boundary-sensitive datasets; decompose gains into trimap boundary vs interior regions.
novelty_hook: Most SAM PEFT targets transformer internals; deliberate neck-only adaptation with boundary-metric analysis seems unexplored; unverified.
kill_risk: The neck's capacity may be too small to express needed corrections, capping gains at trivial levels.

title: Scaling-vector adaptation (SSF-style) matches LoRA on SAM
one_line_idea: Test whether per-channel scale-and-shift vectors match LoRA for SAM adaptation, implying domain gaps are mostly feature re-scaling, not rotation.
problem: LoRA's low-rank rotations may be overkill if segmentation domain shift is dominantly a diagonal (channel-wise gain) phenomenon.
core_hypothesis: Channel-wise affine modulation of frozen features captures the bulk of SAM adaptation gains across moderate shifts.
falsifiable_prediction: Scale-shift vectors reach within a small Dice margin of rank-8 LoRA on several targets while using far fewer parameters, but fail specifically on targets needing new feature mixtures.
why_important: Would identify the algebraic character of segmentation domain shift and set a stronger minimal baseline for all adapter papers.
why_possibly_novel: SSF-style tuning exists for classification; using its success/failure pattern as a probe of what segmentation shift is remains an untested framing; unverified.
minimal_falsification_experiment: Matched-budget comparison of scale-shift vectors, rank-1 LoRA, and rank-8 LoRA across three shift severities with seed replication.
main_risk: The interesting failure cases may be rare in public benchmarks, making the diagnostic claim untestable at scale.
community_default_belief: Low-rank additive updates are the right functional form for adaptation.
why_it_might_be_wrong: That form was chosen for LLM convenience, not derived from any property of visual domain shift.
fastest_falsifying_experiment: One dataset: fit only per-channel scales post-hoc on frozen features against target masks with a frozen decoder; measurable gain already supports the re-scaling view.
core_claim: Channel-wise affine modulation of frozen features captures the bulk of SAM adaptation gains across moderate shifts.
method_sketch: Matched-budget comparison of scale-shift vectors, rank-1 LoRA, and rank-8 LoRA across three shift severities with seed replication.
novelty_hook: SSF-style tuning exists for classification; using its success/failure pattern as a probe of what segmentation shift is remains an untested framing; unverified.
kill_risk: The interesting failure cases may be rare in public benchmarks, making the diagnostic claim untestable at scale.

title: Patch-embedding-only adaptation for modality shift
one_line_idea: For non-RGB modalities (CT windows, ultrasound, SAR), adapt only SAM's patch-embedding convolution, hypothesizing modality gap is concentrated in the first layer.
problem: Whole-encoder adaptation is prescribed for modality shifts that may actually be first-layer input-statistics mismatches.
core_hypothesis: Once pixel statistics are re-encoded into SAM's expected token distribution by a retrained patch embed, the frozen upper network handles the rest for many modalities.
falsifiable_prediction: Patch-embed-only tuning recovers a large fraction of full-LoRA gains on grayscale medical modalities but a small fraction on modalities with different spatial physics such as SAR speckle.
why_important: A first-layer-only recipe would make modality onboarding nearly free and would localize where modality knowledge lives.
why_possibly_novel: Input-layer retuning is folklore in transfer learning; a quantified locus study across medical/radar modalities for promptable segmentation seems missing; unverified.
minimal_falsification_experiment: Across three modalities of increasing physics difference, compare patch-embed-only vs LoRA-everywhere at matched steps; measure token-distribution alignment to source statistics as the mediating variable.
main_risk: Token-distribution alignment may be necessary but far from sufficient, giving uniformly mediocre results.
community_default_belief: Modality shift is deep and requires distributed adaptation through the encoder.
why_it_might_be_wrong: The depth of a shift is usually asserted from failure of zero-shot transfer, which first-layer mismatch alone can fully explain.
fastest_falsifying_experiment: Train patch-embed only on one CT dataset briefly; if Dice stays near frozen-SAM level, concentration in layer one is falsified for CT.
core_claim: Once pixel statistics are re-encoded into SAM's expected token distribution by a retrained patch embed, the frozen upper network handles the rest for many modalities.
method_sketch: Across three modalities of increasing physics difference, compare patch-embed-only vs LoRA-everywhere at matched steps; measure token-distribution alignment to source statistics as the mediating variable.
novelty_hook: Input-layer retuning is folklore in transfer learning; a quantified locus study across medical/radar modalities for promptable segmentation seems missing; unverified.
kill_risk: Token-distribution alignment may be necessary but far from sufficient, giving uniformly mediocre results.

title: When nonlinearity in adapters is actually needed
one_line_idea: Characterize the boundary between targets where linear LoRA suffices and targets where nonlinear bottleneck adapters are required for SAM.
problem: Linear and nonlinear adapter families are used interchangeably with no theory of which target properties demand nonlinearity.
core_hypothesis: Nonlinear adapters only pay off when the target requires qualitatively new boundary types or grouping rules, not for appearance re-statistics.
falsifiable_prediction: On appearance-shifted targets, linear LoRA ties nonlinear adapters at matched budgets; on targets with novel structure (thin vessels, nested parts), nonlinear adapters show a consistent margin.
why_important: Gives practitioners a principled architecture choice and probes what kind of function class domain adaptation of dense predictors is.
why_possibly_novel: Linear-vs-nonlinear PEFT comparisons exist piecemeal; a target-property-conditioned characterization for segmentation is plausibly new; unverified.
minimal_falsification_experiment: A 2x2 study: {linear, nonlinear adapter} x {appearance-shift, structure-shift datasets}, matched budgets, boundary and topology-aware metrics.
main_risk: Defining and operationalizing 'structure shift' cleanly may be harder than the experiment itself.
community_default_belief: Adapter nonlinearity is a minor architectural flavor without systematic consequences.
why_it_might_be_wrong: Function-approximation arguments suggest linear updates cannot create genuinely new decision boundaries in frozen feature space.
fastest_falsifying_experiment: Pick one thin-structure dataset; if linear LoRA matches a nonlinear adapter there at equal budget, the conditional theory loses its strongest case.
core_claim: Nonlinear adapters only pay off when the target requires qualitatively new boundary types or grouping rules, not for appearance re-statistics.
method_sketch: A 2x2 study: {linear, nonlinear adapter} x {appearance-shift, structure-shift datasets}, matched budgets, boundary and topology-aware metrics.
novelty_hook: Linear-vs-nonlinear PEFT comparisons exist piecemeal; a target-property-conditioned characterization for segmentation is plausibly new; unverified.
kill_risk: Defining and operationalizing 'structure shift' cleanly may be harder than the experiment itself.

title: Layer-shared (tied) LoRA exploits ViT redundancy
one_line_idea: Share a single LoRA module across all SAM encoder blocks, betting that inter-layer redundancy makes per-layer adapters wasteful.
problem: Adapter parameter count scales linearly with depth even though ViT blocks are known to be highly correlated in function.
core_hypothesis: One weight-tied adapter applied at every block captures most of the adaptation expressed by independent per-layer adapters.
falsifiable_prediction: Tied LoRA achieves at least 90% of per-layer LoRA's Dice gain with roughly 1/depth of the parameters across several targets.
why_important: Constant-size adapters would make storing hundreds of domain adapters trivial for multi-tenant segmentation services.
why_possibly_novel: Weight tying across layers appears in efficient-transformer work; as a SAM adaptation strategy with a redundancy argument it seems untested; unverified.
minimal_falsification_experiment: Train tied vs untied LoRA at both equal-per-layer-rank and equal-total-parameter settings on three datasets; also measure cosine similarity between independently learned per-layer adapters as supporting evidence.
main_risk: Depth-specific corrections (early texture vs late semantics) may be exactly what adaptation needs, which tying forbids.
community_default_belief: Each layer needs its own adaptation degrees of freedom.
why_it_might_be_wrong: If learned per-layer adapters turn out to be highly similar to each other, the per-layer freedom is demonstrably unused.
fastest_falsifying_experiment: Measure pairwise similarity of per-layer LoRA updates from one existing training run; near-orthogonal updates across layers falsify the redundancy premise cheaply.
core_claim: One weight-tied adapter applied at every block captures most of the adaptation expressed by independent per-layer adapters.
method_sketch: Train tied vs untied LoRA at both equal-per-layer-rank and equal-total-parameter settings on three datasets; also measure cosine similarity between independently learned per-layer adapters as supporting evidence.
novelty_hook: Weight tying across layers appears in efficient-transformer work; as a SAM adaptation strategy with a redundancy argument it seems untested; unverified.
kill_risk: Depth-specific corrections (early texture vs late semantics) may be exactly what adaptation needs, which tying forbids.

title: Task-prompt tokens instead of weight updates
one_line_idea: Adapt SAM by learning a small set of auxiliary prompt tokens appended to the sparse prompt embeddings, leaving all weights frozen.
problem: Weight-space PEFT alters the model globally, while many adaptations may only need to tell the decoder what kind of thing to segment.
core_hypothesis: A handful of learned task tokens fed through the existing prompt pathway can steer the frozen decoder to domain-appropriate masks for moderate shifts.
falsifiable_prediction: Learned task tokens recover a meaningful fraction of decoder-fine-tuning gains on in-modality domain shifts, and near zero on modality shifts, at under a few thousand trainable parameters.
why_important: Prompt-token adaptation is deployable without touching model files, enabling per-user or per-class customization in shared inference services.
why_possibly_novel: Prompt tuning is standard in NLP and exists for vision transformers; routing it specifically through SAM's sparse-prompt interface as the sole adaptation channel is plausibly less charted; unverified.
minimal_falsification_experiment: Freeze SAM entirely, learn k task tokens per target dataset by gradient descent through the prompt encoder pathway, sweep k, compare to decoder-only tuning.
main_risk: The prompt bottleneck may be too narrow to carry domain information, capping gains at cosmetic levels.
community_default_belief: Serious adaptation requires modifying weights somewhere in the network.
why_it_might_be_wrong: SAM was explicitly built to be steered by prompts, so its prompt channel may have far more unexplored control bandwidth than assumed.
fastest_falsifying_experiment: Learn tokens on one dataset for an hour of GPU time; if training loss cannot even fit the training set, the channel is too narrow and the idea dies.
core_claim: A handful of learned task tokens fed through the existing prompt pathway can steer the frozen decoder to domain-appropriate masks for moderate shifts.
method_sketch: Freeze SAM entirely, learn k task tokens per target dataset by gradient descent through the prompt encoder pathway, sweep k, compare to decoder-only tuning.
novelty_hook: Prompt tuning is standard in NLP and exists for vision transformers; routing it specifically through SAM's sparse-prompt interface as the sole adaptation channel is plausibly less charted; unverified.
kill_risk: The prompt bottleneck may be too narrow to carry domain information, capping gains at cosmetic levels.

title: Prompt-embedding recalibration for shifted geometry
one_line_idea: Learn a tiny MLP that re-maps SAM's point/box prompt embeddings for a target domain, restoring the click-to-mask geometry that domain shift breaks.
problem: Under domain shift, the same click produces systematically wrong mask extents, suggesting the prompt-to-feature correspondence, not the features, is miscalibrated.
core_hypothesis: A learned low-capacity transform on prompt embeddings corrects systematic click-response biases without touching image features.
falsifiable_prediction: Prompt recalibration alone reduces the number of clicks needed to reach a target IoU on shifted domains, with zero change on in-domain images.
why_important: Interactive annotation efficiency is the actual currency of SAM in production labeling pipelines; a clicks-to-IoU reduction is directly valuable.
why_possibly_novel: Adaptation work targets features or decoders; treating the prompt embedding map itself as the miscalibrated component appears to be an unusual locus; unverified.
minimal_falsification_experiment: Simulate standard iterative clicking on a shifted dataset with and without a trained prompt-recalibration MLP; compare clicks-to-90%-IoU curves.
main_risk: Click-response errors may be image-content-dependent in ways a global prompt transform cannot express.
community_default_belief: Interactive degradation under shift is a feature-quality problem requiring encoder adaptation.
why_it_might_be_wrong: Systematic biases (masks consistently too large/small in a domain) look like calibration errors, which are cheaply correctable at the interface.
fastest_falsifying_experiment: Measure whether click-response errors on one shifted dataset are systematic (biased) vs random; unbiased errors falsify the calibration framing before any training.
core_claim: A learned low-capacity transform on prompt embeddings corrects systematic click-response biases without touching image features.
method_sketch: Simulate standard iterative clicking on a shifted dataset with and without a trained prompt-recalibration MLP; compare clicks-to-90%-IoU curves.
novelty_hook: Adaptation work targets features or decoders; treating the prompt embedding map itself as the miscalibrated component appears to be an unusual locus; unverified.
kill_risk: Click-response errors may be image-content-dependent in ways a global prompt transform cannot express.

title: Learned negative-prompt vocabulary for background suppression
one_line_idea: Learn reusable negative-prompt embeddings representing domain-specific distractors (e.g., 'ultrasound shadow', 'slide artifact') that users or pipelines can invoke without weight changes.
problem: SAM supports negative clicks but has no notion of reusable, named background concepts that plague specific domains.
core_hypothesis: A small learned vocabulary of negative embeddings suppresses recurring false-positive structures more efficiently than per-image negative clicking.
falsifiable_prediction: Injecting one learned domain-negative token reduces false-positive area on recurring distractor structures by more than an equivalent budget of simulated negative clicks.
why_important: Recurring distractors dominate correction effort in real annotation; amortizing them into reusable tokens attacks the actual cost center.
why_possibly_novel: Negative prompting exists per-interaction; a persistent learned negative vocabulary per domain appears unexplored for SAM; unverified.
minimal_falsification_experiment: Identify a recurring distractor class in one dataset, learn a negative token against it, and evaluate FP-area reduction and Dice on held-out images vs click-matched baselines.
main_risk: Negative tokens may bleed into suppressing true-positive regions with similar appearance.
community_default_belief: Negative information is inherently per-image and must come from interactive clicks.
why_it_might_be_wrong: Domain distractors are strongly stereotyped (shadows, coils, bubbles), which is exactly what a learned embedding can encode once.
fastest_falsifying_experiment: Train one negative token on one distractor type for a few hours; no FP reduction on held-out images kills it.
core_claim: A small learned vocabulary of negative embeddings suppresses recurring false-positive structures more efficiently than per-image negative clicking.
method_sketch: Identify a recurring distractor class in one dataset, learn a negative token against it, and evaluate FP-area reduction and Dice on held-out images vs click-matched baselines.
novelty_hook: Negative prompting exists per-interaction; a persistent learned negative vocabulary per domain appears unexplored for SAM; unverified.
kill_risk: Negative tokens may bleed into suppressing true-positive regions with similar appearance.

title: Mask-token cloning for semantic specialization
one_line_idea: Clone SAM's output mask tokens and fine-tune each clone for one target class, converting the class-agnostic decoder into a semantic segmenter with a few thousand parameters.
problem: Turning SAM semantic usually bolts on external classifiers or full decoders, ignoring that mask tokens already select what to segment.
core_hypothesis: Per-class mask-token specialization plus a frozen decoder yields competitive semantic segmentation for small class vocabularies.
falsifiable_prediction: With under ten classes, tuned mask-token clones reach a large fraction of a fully fine-tuned decoder's mIoU while training four orders of magnitude fewer parameters.
why_important: It would be the cheapest known path from promptable to semantic segmentation, ideal for embedded or per-customer class sets.
why_possibly_novel: Query-token specialization echoes DETR-style query learning; applying it to SAM's mask tokens as the sole trained component seems fresh; unverified.
minimal_falsification_experiment: On one multi-class dataset, train class-specific token clones with everything frozen; compare mIoU to decoder fine-tuning and to linear-probe baselines.
main_risk: Mask tokens may encode mask style rather than content selection, in which case clones cannot become class-selective.
community_default_belief: Class semantics must be injected via text encoders or trained heads, not via SAM's own output tokens.
why_it_might_be_wrong: The decoder's tokens already produce systematically different mask granularities, evidence they carry selectable intent.
fastest_falsifying_experiment: Optimize a single token clone for one class on a small dataset; failure to become class-selective within a day of compute is decisive.
core_claim: Per-class mask-token specialization plus a frozen decoder yields competitive semantic segmentation for small class vocabularies.
method_sketch: On one multi-class dataset, train class-specific token clones with everything frozen; compare mIoU to decoder fine-tuning and to linear-probe baselines.
novelty_hook: Query-token specialization echoes DETR-style query learning; applying it to SAM's mask tokens as the sole trained component seems fresh; unverified.
kill_risk: Mask tokens may encode mask style rather than content selection, in which case clones cannot become class-selective.

title: IoU-head recalibration as first-line domain adaptation
one_line_idea: Recalibrate only SAM's mask-quality (IoU) head on the target domain so mask ranking and downstream selection work, before touching any mask-producing weights.
problem: Under domain shift SAM often produces a usable mask among its candidates but ranks it wrong, so pipelines pick bad masks even when good ones exist.
core_hypothesis: A recalibrated quality head recovers a meaningful share of end-task performance by fixing selection, at near-zero cost and zero risk to mask quality.
falsifiable_prediction: Oracle-choice analysis shows a persistent gap between best-candidate and chosen-candidate IoU on shifted domains, and quality-head recalibration closes most of that gap.
why_important: It separates 'SAM cannot segment this' from 'SAM cannot rank this', a distinction the adaptation literature conflates when reporting failures.
why_possibly_novel: Everyone tunes the mask path; treating the scoring head as the primary broken component with an oracle-gap methodology seems uncommon; unverified.
minimal_falsification_experiment: On two shifted datasets, compute oracle-vs-selected candidate gaps, then fine-tune only the IoU head and remeasure end-task Dice and selection accuracy.
main_risk: On hard domains all candidates may be bad, making better ranking worthless.
community_default_belief: SAM's failures under shift are mask-generation failures, so adaptation must change mask production.
why_it_might_be_wrong: Candidate diversity from multimask output is substantial, and nobody routinely checks whether a good candidate was available but unchosen.
fastest_falsifying_experiment: Pure analysis, no training: measure the oracle-selection gap on one shifted dataset; a small gap falsifies the premise immediately.
core_claim: A recalibrated quality head recovers a meaningful share of end-task performance by fixing selection, at near-zero cost and zero risk to mask quality.
method_sketch: On two shifted datasets, compute oracle-vs-selected candidate gaps, then fine-tune only the IoU head and remeasure end-task Dice and selection accuracy.
novelty_hook: Everyone tunes the mask path; treating the scoring head as the primary broken component with an oracle-gap methodology seems uncommon; unverified.
kill_risk: On hard domains all candidates may be bad, making better ranking worthless.

title: Learned dense prompt priors per domain
one_line_idea: Learn a fixed dense (mask-like) prompt map per target domain that is always fed to SAM's dense prompt input, encoding where objects tend to be and how boundaries behave.
problem: SAM's dense-prompt channel is nearly unused in adaptation work even though it is a natural carrier for domain-level spatial priors.
core_hypothesis: A learned static or image-statistic-conditioned dense prior improves shifted-domain segmentation without weight updates, especially for anatomically stereotyped layouts.
falsifiable_prediction: On datasets with strong layout regularity (e.g., organ position in axial slices), a learned dense prior yields consistent Dice gains, while on layout-random datasets it gives none.
why_important: Exploits an existing, cheap input interface for adaptation and quantifies how much domain knowledge is pure spatial prior.
why_possibly_novel: Dense-prompt learning as a standalone adaptation channel for SAM appears rarely studied compared to sparse prompts; unverified.
minimal_falsification_experiment: Learn a dense prior per dataset with SAM frozen on two layout-regular and one layout-random dataset; ablate static vs image-conditioned priors.
main_risk: The decoder may treat dense prompts as weak hints, attenuating any learned signal below usefulness.
community_default_belief: Adaptation-relevant information is in features and weights, not in a spatial prior injectable at the prompt interface.
why_it_might_be_wrong: In stereotyped domains a large fraction of segmentation information is literally positional, which this channel can carry directly.
fastest_falsifying_experiment: Feed the dataset-mean mask as a dense prompt with frozen SAM; any measurable gain on a layout-regular dataset validates the channel in minutes.
core_claim: A learned static or image-statistic-conditioned dense prior improves shifted-domain segmentation without weight updates, especially for anatomically stereotyped layouts.
method_sketch: Learn a dense prior per dataset with SAM frozen on two layout-regular and one layout-random dataset; ablate static vs image-conditioned priors.
novelty_hook: Dense-prompt learning as a standalone adaptation channel for SAM appears rarely studied compared to sparse prompts; unverified.
kill_risk: The decoder may treat dense prompts as weak hints, attenuating any learned signal below usefulness.

title: Decoder cross-attention LoRA for interactive medical use
one_line_idea: Place LoRA only inside the mask decoder's two-way transformer cross-attention, adapting how prompts read image features rather than the features themselves.
problem: Interactive medical segmentation degrades under shift, and it is unknown whether the prompt-to-image reading operation or the image representation is at fault.
core_hypothesis: Adapting only the decoder's cross-attention restores most interactive (click-based) performance on shifted domains because the reading operation, not the representation, is what breaks.
falsifiable_prediction: Decoder cross-attention LoRA improves clicks-to-target-IoU substantially more than parameter-matched encoder LoRA in interactive evaluation, while encoder LoRA wins in single-shot automatic evaluation.
why_important: Separates interactive from automatic adaptation needs, which matters because annotation tooling is SAM's dominant real use.
why_possibly_novel: Ablations of decoder components exist, but an interactive-vs-automatic dissociation study of adaptation locus appears untried; unverified.
minimal_falsification_experiment: Train decoder-cross-attention-only and encoder-only LoRA on one medical dataset; evaluate both under simulated iterative clicking and single-prompt protocols.
main_risk: Both loci may be entangled so that neither shows a clean dissociation.
community_default_belief: One adaptation locus should serve both automatic and interactive use cases.
why_it_might_be_wrong: The two use cases exercise disjoint computation paths (prompt-conditioned reading vs feature encoding), so their failure modes need not coincide.
fastest_falsifying_experiment: On a shifted dataset, check whether interactive failures persist when ground-truth-guided optimal prompts are given; if optimal prompts already fix everything, the reading operation is fine and the hypothesis dies.
core_claim: Adapting only the decoder's cross-attention restores most interactive (click-based) performance on shifted domains because the reading operation, not the representation, is what breaks.
method_sketch: Train decoder-cross-attention-only and encoder-only LoRA on one medical dataset; evaluate both under simulated iterative clicking and single-prompt protocols.
novelty_hook: Ablations of decoder components exist, but an interactive-vs-automatic dissociation study of adaptation locus appears untried; unverified.
kill_risk: Both loci may be entangled so that neither shows a clean dissociation.

title: Train adapters under iterative-click curricula
one_line_idea: Fine-tune SAM adapters inside a simulated multi-round clicking loop instead of the standard single-prompt supervised setup.
problem: Adapters are trained one-shot but deployed in iterative human-in-the-loop correction, a train/deploy mismatch nobody prices in.
core_hypothesis: Training with simulated correction rounds teaches adapters to be correctable, improving real interactive efficiency even when one-shot Dice is unchanged.
falsifiable_prediction: Curriculum-trained adapters need fewer clicks to reach fixed IoU thresholds than one-shot-trained adapters of identical architecture, despite similar single-prompt Dice.
why_important: Clicks saved per image is the metric annotation teams actually pay for, and it is invisible to standard benchmarks.
why_possibly_novel: Iterative training exists in interactive-segmentation literature pre-SAM; porting it as a PEFT training protocol with correctability as the outcome seems underexplored for SAM; unverified.
minimal_falsification_experiment: Same adapter, two training protocols (one-shot vs simulated 3-round clicking), evaluated with a standardized click simulator on two datasets, reporting clicks-to-IoU.
main_risk: Click simulators may diverge from human behavior enough that gains do not transfer to real annotators.
community_default_belief: Optimizing single-prompt accuracy automatically optimizes interactive workflows.
why_it_might_be_wrong: Correctability (how outputs respond to a corrective click) is a distinct functional property that one-shot losses never supervise.
fastest_falsifying_experiment: Evaluate an existing one-shot-trained adapter under iterative clicking: if its correction responses are already near-monotone improvements, there is no correctability headroom to gain.
core_claim: Training with simulated correction rounds teaches adapters to be correctable, improving real interactive efficiency even when one-shot Dice is unchanged.
method_sketch: Same adapter, two training protocols (one-shot vs simulated 3-round clicking), evaluated with a standardized click simulator on two datasets, reporting clicks-to-IoU.
novelty_hook: Iterative training exists in interactive-segmentation literature pre-SAM; porting it as a PEFT training protocol with correctability as the outcome seems underexplored for SAM; unverified.
kill_risk: Click simulators may diverge from human behavior enough that gains do not transfer to real annotators.

title: Promptability drift as a first-class PEFT metric
one_line_idea: Define and measure 'promptability drift'—how much an adapted SAM's response to canonical prompts changes on generic images—and use it as a regularization target during PEFT.
problem: Adaptation papers report target-domain gains but almost never quantify what interactive ability was destroyed elsewhere.
core_hypothesis: Promptability drift varies enormously across PEFT methods at equal target accuracy, and constraining it costs little target performance.
falsifiable_prediction: Across common PEFT recipes at matched target Dice, drift on a fixed generic prompt suite varies by a large factor, and a drift-penalized variant retains most target gains with a fraction of the drift.
why_important: Makes the hidden cost of adaptation visible and optimizable, enabling adapted models that remain safe general-purpose tools.
why_possibly_novel: Catastrophic forgetting metrics exist for classes; a prompt-response-centric drift metric tailored to promptable models seems unformalized; unverified.
minimal_falsification_experiment: Build a fixed suite of images+prompts, define drift as mask IoU between frozen and adapted models, profile several PEFT methods, then add drift as a training penalty and measure the trade-off curve.
main_risk: Drift may correlate almost perfectly with target gain, making the trade-off curve trivial and the metric redundant.
community_default_belief: Zero-shot degradation from PEFT is minor because so few weights change.
why_it_might_be_wrong: Low-rank changes at strategic points can globally redirect attention; parameter count is a poor proxy for functional change.
fastest_falsifying_experiment: Measure drift for two published adapter checkpoints (or quick retrains) on 50 generic images; if both are negligible the concern is empirically hollow.
core_claim: Promptability drift varies enormously across PEFT methods at equal target accuracy, and constraining it costs little target performance.
method_sketch: Build a fixed suite of images+prompts, define drift as mask IoU between frozen and adapted models, profile several PEFT methods, then add drift as a training penalty and measure the trade-off curve.
novelty_hook: Catastrophic forgetting metrics exist for classes; a prompt-response-centric drift metric tailored to promptable models seems unformalized; unverified.
kill_risk: Drift may correlate almost perfectly with target gain, making the trade-off curve trivial and the metric redundant.

title: Hypernetwork prompt-token generation from support sets
one_line_idea: Train a small hypernetwork that maps a few support image-mask pairs to SAM prompt tokens, enabling in-context segmentation of novel classes with all SAM weights frozen.
problem: Per-dataset PEFT requires a training loop per target, while many users have only a handful of examples and no training infrastructure.
core_hypothesis: Class identity for segmentation can be compressed into SAM's prompt-token space by an amortized encoder, generalizing to unseen classes.
falsifiable_prediction: A support-conditioned token generator trained on a broad class mixture outperforms per-class prompt tuning when examples are fewer than ~10, and generalizes above chance to held-out class families.
why_important: Amortized adaptation would replace thousands of fine-tuning jobs with one forward pass, changing how SAM is deployed for long-tail classes.
why_possibly_novel: In-context segmentation exists in other architectures; distilling it into the native prompt interface of a frozen SAM appears less explored; unverified.
minimal_falsification_experiment: Train the hypernetwork on a multi-class corpus with episodic sampling; test on held-out classes against per-class prompt tuning and fine-tuned baselines under a fixed shot budget.
main_risk: Prompt-token space may lack capacity to encode class concepts that were never separable in SAM's pretraining.
community_default_belief: Few-shot adaptation of segmentation models requires gradient steps on the new data.
why_it_might_be_wrong: Amortization has repeatedly replaced inner-loop optimization once the conditioning interface is right, and SAM's prompt space is a purpose-built conditioning interface.
fastest_falsifying_experiment: Overfit the hypernetwork on 5 classes; if generated tokens cannot even match per-class tuned tokens on training classes, the interface lacks capacity.
core_claim: Class identity for segmentation can be compressed into SAM's prompt-token space by an amortized encoder, generalizing to unseen classes.
method_sketch: Train the hypernetwork on a multi-class corpus with episodic sampling; test on held-out classes against per-class prompt tuning and fine-tuned baselines under a fixed shot budget.
novelty_hook: In-context segmentation exists in other architectures; distilling it into the native prompt interface of a frozen SAM appears less explored; unverified.
kill_risk: Prompt-token space may lack capacity to encode class concepts that were never separable in SAM's pretraining.

title: Class-query tokens turn SAM panoptic at negligible cost
one_line_idea: Attach a learned set of class-query tokens that run through SAM's decoder in everything-mode, producing panoptic-style labeled masks with only the queries and a tiny classifier trained.
problem: Panoptic/semantic outputs from SAM currently require external classifiers per mask or heavyweight added decoders.
core_hypothesis: The decoder can serve query-based semantic readout natively, so a query set plus linear classifier achieves usable panoptic quality with the backbone and decoder frozen.
falsifiable_prediction: On a modest-vocabulary dataset, query-token panoptic readout reaches a meaningful fraction of a trained panoptic head's PQ at under 1% of its trainable parameters.
why_important: It would collapse the promptable-to-panoptic gap into a token-learning problem, ideal for resource-limited teams.
why_possibly_novel: Combines DETR-style queries with a frozen promptable decoder; this specific frozen-decoder readout seems untested; unverified.
minimal_falsification_experiment: Train class queries plus a linear class head on one panoptic dataset with SAM frozen; compare PQ against mask-classification baselines at matched supervision.
main_risk: Everything-mode mask proposals may systematically miss stuff-classes, capping PQ regardless of query quality.
community_default_belief: Panoptic segmentation needs task-specific decoders trained end-to-end.
why_it_might_be_wrong: Frozen proposal quality from SAM is already high; the missing piece may be only labeling, which queries can supply.
fastest_falsifying_experiment: Measure oracle PQ of frozen SAM everything-mode proposals on the target dataset; a low oracle ceiling falsifies the approach before training anything.
core_claim: The decoder can serve query-based semantic readout natively, so a query set plus linear classifier achieves usable panoptic quality with the backbone and decoder frozen.
method_sketch: Train class queries plus a linear class head on one panoptic dataset with SAM frozen; compare PQ against mask-classification baselines at matched supervision.
novelty_hook: Combines DETR-style queries with a frozen promptable decoder; this specific frozen-decoder readout seems untested; unverified.
kill_risk: Everything-mode mask proposals may systematically miss stuff-classes, capping PQ regardless of query quality.

title: A shift-taxonomy that predicts the right PEFT locus
one_line_idea: Build a taxonomy mapping domain-shift type (texture, scale, topology, physics) to the empirically best SAM adaptation locus, tested prospectively on unseen domains.
problem: Every new domain restarts the which-PEFT-where search from scratch because no predictive theory connects shift character to adaptation placement.
core_hypothesis: A small set of measurable shift descriptors (frequency-spectrum distance, object-scale statistics, boundary curvature distributions) predicts which PEFT configuration wins on a new domain.
falsifiable_prediction: A rule fit on N seen domains selects the best-of-k PEFT configuration on held-out domains significantly better than always choosing the overall-best single configuration.
why_important: Converts PEFT recipe selection from per-domain search into a measurement-driven lookup, saving the community large amounts of redundant tuning.
why_possibly_novel: Meta-analyses of PEFT exist; a prospective, descriptor-based locus-prediction rule for segmentation seems absent; unverified.
minimal_falsification_experiment: Run a fixed grid of PEFT configurations across 8-10 diverse public segmentation domains, fit a predictor from shift descriptors to best configuration, validate leave-one-domain-out.
main_risk: Best-configuration labels may be noisy at feasible compute, drowning the signal the taxonomy needs.
community_default_belief: PEFT choice is an empirical per-dataset matter without transferable structure.
why_it_might_be_wrong: The same physical causes of shift recur across domains, so their remedies plausibly recur too; nobody has organized the evidence to check.
fastest_falsifying_experiment: For two obviously different shift types, check whether the best-of-3 PEFT configuration differs at all; identical winners everywhere would undermine the premise cheaply.
core_claim: A small set of measurable shift descriptors (frequency-spectrum distance, object-scale statistics, boundary curvature distributions) predicts which PEFT configuration wins on a new domain.
method_sketch: Run a fixed grid of PEFT configurations across 8-10 diverse public segmentation domains, fit a predictor from shift descriptors to best configuration, validate leave-one-domain-out.
novelty_hook: Meta-analyses of PEFT exist; a prospective, descriptor-based locus-prediction rule for segmentation seems absent; unverified.
kill_risk: Best-configuration labels may be noisy at feasible compute, drowning the signal the taxonomy needs.

title: Frequency-domain adapters for ultrasound speckle
one_line_idea: Adapt SAM to ultrasound with adapters that operate on frequency-band decompositions of early features, targeting speckle as a multiplicative-noise phenomenon.
problem: Ultrasound speckle violates the additive natural-image statistics SAM saw in pretraining, and spatial-domain adapters may fight it inefficiently.
core_hypothesis: Speckle-induced degradation is concentrated in specific spatial-frequency bands of early features, so band-targeted low-rank modulation beats generic spatial LoRA per parameter.
falsifiable_prediction: Frequency-band adapters at equal parameter count outperform standard LoRA on ultrasound targets, while showing no advantage on non-speckle modalities like CT.
why_important: Ultrasound is among the most-used and most-shifted clinical modalities; a physics-matched adapter form would be broadly reusable.
why_possibly_novel: Frequency-aware adaptation modules exist in restoration; importing them as PEFT for promptable segmentation of speckle imagery seems untried; unverified.
minimal_falsification_experiment: Implement FFT-gated adapters on early SAM blocks; compare against parameter-matched LoRA on two public ultrasound segmentation datasets and one CT control.
main_risk: Speckle's effect on deep features may already be diffuse across bands, removing the concentration the design assumes.
community_default_belief: Generic adapters handle any modality given enough data; noise physics does not require architectural acknowledgment.
why_it_might_be_wrong: Multiplicative noise has strong known spectral structure, and generic adapters must spend capacity rediscovering what a frequency decomposition provides for free.
fastest_falsifying_experiment: Measure frozen-SAM feature divergence between ultrasound and natural images per frequency band; a flat divergence profile falsifies the concentration premise without training.
core_claim: Speckle-induced degradation is concentrated in specific spatial-frequency bands of early features, so band-targeted low-rank modulation beats generic spatial LoRA per parameter.
method_sketch: Implement FFT-gated adapters on early SAM blocks; compare against parameter-matched LoRA on two public ultrasound segmentation datasets and one CT control.
novelty_hook: Frequency-aware adaptation modules exist in restoration; importing them as PEFT for promptable segmentation of speckle imagery seems untried; unverified.
kill_risk: Speckle's effect on deep features may already be diffuse across bands, removing the concentration the design assumes.

title: Stain-and-scale-only adaptation for histopathology
one_line_idea: Adapt SAM to pathology slides by tuning only the patch embedding (stain statistics) and positional/scale handling, testing whether the celebrated pathology domain gap is mostly these two factors.
problem: Pathology adaptation methods are heavyweight, but the modality's dominant nuisances—stain variation and magnification—are low-dimensional and localized.
core_hypothesis: Patch-embed plus scale-handling adaptation captures most of the achievable PEFT gain on H&E segmentation tasks, with deeper adaptation adding little.
falsifiable_prediction: The two-locus recipe reaches within a small margin of full-encoder LoRA on nuclei/gland segmentation, and the residual gap correlates with tasks requiring tissue-level context rather than appearance.
why_important: Pathology deployments span thousands of scanners and stains; a two-knob adaptation would be operationally transformative and scientifically clarifying.
why_possibly_novel: Stain normalization is classic; framing it as a locus-sufficiency claim inside SAM PEFT with a context-vs-appearance residual analysis seems new; unverified.
minimal_falsification_experiment: On public nuclei and gland segmentation datasets, compare frozen, stain+scale-loci, full LoRA, and stain-normalization-preprocessing baselines under one protocol.
main_risk: Gland-level tasks may need relational context adaptation that the two loci cannot express, making the claim task-dependent in an uninteresting way.
community_default_belief: Pathology is a deep domain gap requiring pathology-specific foundation models or extensive fine-tuning.
why_it_might_be_wrong: The gap has rarely been decomposed; its apparent depth may be an artifact of entangling two shallow nuisances.
fastest_falsifying_experiment: Apply classical stain normalization plus correct rescaling and evaluate frozen SAM; if zero-shot performance jumps substantially, shallow-nuisance dominance is supported within hours.
core_claim: Patch-embed plus scale-handling adaptation captures most of the achievable PEFT gain on H&E segmentation tasks, with deeper adaptation adding little.
method_sketch: On public nuclei and gland segmentation datasets, compare frozen, stain+scale-loci, full LoRA, and stain-normalization-preprocessing baselines under one protocol.
novelty_hook: Stain normalization is classic; framing it as a locus-sufficiency claim inside SAM PEFT with a context-vs-appearance residual analysis seems new; unverified.
kill_risk: Gland-level tasks may need relational context adaptation that the two loci cannot express, making the claim task-dependent in an uninteresting way.

title: Learned tiling policies beat weight adaptation for aerial tiny objects
one_line_idea: For remote-sensing small-object segmentation, learn a content-aware tiling/zoom policy that feeds SAM optimally sized crops, and test it against weight-space PEFT at matched budgets.
problem: SAM misses tiny aerial objects mainly because of resolution handling, yet the community's reflex is to fine-tune weights rather than fix what the model is shown.
core_hypothesis: A lightweight policy choosing crop size and overlap per region recovers more tiny-object recall than parameter-matched LoRA, because the bottleneck is input evidence, not features.
falsifiable_prediction: Policy-driven tiling with frozen SAM exceeds LoRA-adapted SAM at native tiling on small-object recall, while LoRA wins only when tiling is fixed for both.
why_important: Reframes a whole class of 'domain gaps' as observation-policy problems, which are cheaper, interpretable, and model-agnostic.
why_possibly_novel: Adaptive tiling exists in detection engineering; posing tiling-policy-vs-PEFT as a controlled scientific comparison seems unposed; unverified.
minimal_falsification_experiment: Train a small policy network (or tune a heuristic) for crop selection on one aerial dataset; compare against LoRA under equal added compute, reporting recall by object size.
main_risk: Compute-matched comparison is tricky because tiling multiplies inference cost in ways adapter training does not.
community_default_belief: Small-object failure is a representational deficiency to be fixed by fine-tuning.
why_it_might_be_wrong: At sufficient zoom SAM often segments the same objects fine, indicating the deficiency is in what it sees, not what it knows.
fastest_falsifying_experiment: Manually zoom failing cases on one dataset: if frozen SAM still fails on centered, enlarged tiny objects, the observation-policy framing collapses.
core_claim: A lightweight policy choosing crop size and overlap per region recovers more tiny-object recall than parameter-matched LoRA, because the bottleneck is input evidence, not features.
method_sketch: Train a small policy network (or tune a heuristic) for crop selection on one aerial dataset; compare against LoRA under equal added compute, reporting recall by object size.
novelty_hook: Adaptive tiling exists in detection engineering; posing tiling-policy-vs-PEFT as a controlled scientific comparison seems unposed; unverified.
kill_risk: Compute-matched comparison is tricky because tiling multiplies inference cost in ways adapter training does not.

title: Learned pseudo-colorization front-ends for SAR and thermal
one_line_idea: Adapt SAM to SAR/thermal imagery through a small trainable pseudo-colorization network at the input, competing against in-model PEFT.
problem: Single-channel physics-different modalities are shoved through RGB-pretrained encoders with naive channel replication, then heavy PEFT compensates inside the network.
core_hypothesis: A learned input mapping into SAM's expected color-texture manifold moves much of the adaptation outside the model, matching encoder LoRA on these modalities.
falsifiable_prediction: Input-network adaptation (frozen SAM) performs within a small margin of encoder LoRA on thermal targets, with larger residual gaps on SAR where spatial statistics differ, and composes additively with light LoRA.
why_important: Input-space adaptation keeps one shared frozen backbone for all modalities, simplifying certification and multi-modal serving.
why_possibly_novel: Learned input transforms are an old idea; a quantified input-vs-weight adaptation decomposition for promptable segmentation on radar/thermal seems missing; unverified.
minimal_falsification_experiment: Train a 3-layer conv front-end vs rank-matched LoRA vs both, on one thermal and one SAR public dataset, single protocol, seeds.
main_risk: SAR geometry effects (layover, foreshortening) are not appearance problems and may defeat any input-space remedy.
community_default_belief: Modality gaps of this size necessarily require adapting the representation, not the input.
why_it_might_be_wrong: The encoder never sees raw physics, only pixel statistics; matching those statistics may be sufficient for the encoder to reuse its machinery.
fastest_falsifying_experiment: Fit the front-end alone for a few epochs on thermal data; if Dice remains at frozen-baseline level the input channel is insufficient there.
core_claim: A learned input mapping into SAM's expected color-texture manifold moves much of the adaptation outside the model, matching encoder LoRA on these modalities.
method_sketch: Train a 3-layer conv front-end vs rank-matched LoRA vs both, on one thermal and one SAR public dataset, single protocol, seeds.
novelty_hook: Learned input transforms are an old idea; a quantified input-vs-weight adaptation decomposition for promptable segmentation on radar/thermal seems missing; unverified.
kill_risk: SAR geometry effects (layover, foreshortening) are not appearance problems and may defeat any input-space remedy.

title: Camouflage exposes the limits of low-rank adaptation
one_line_idea: Use camouflaged-object segmentation as a stress test to establish which failure classes low-rank PEFT fundamentally cannot fix in SAM.
problem: PEFT is applied indiscriminately without any established negative result delineating what it cannot repair.
core_hypothesis: Camouflage failures stem from grouping decisions in attention that low-rank additive updates cannot re-route, so LoRA at any practical rank plateaus far below full fine-tuning on camouflage benchmarks.
falsifiable_prediction: The LoRA-vs-full-fine-tune gap on camouflaged-object datasets remains large across ranks up to hundreds, while the same sweep closes the gap on ordinary domain shifts.
why_important: A credible boundary of PEFT applicability would save the field from misapplied adapters and identify where new mechanisms are genuinely required.
why_possibly_novel: Rank-sweep saturation analyses exist for LLMs; a task-family-specific PEFT impossibility claim in segmentation appears unmade; unverified.
minimal_falsification_experiment: Rank sweep (4 to 256) vs full fine-tuning on one camouflage dataset and one ordinary-shift control, plotting gap-vs-rank saturation curves.
main_risk: The gap may close at high ranks, converting the impossibility claim into a mundane capacity statement.
community_default_belief: With enough rank, LoRA approximates full fine-tuning for any target.
why_it_might_be_wrong: The approximation argument concerns weights, not optimization: gradient trajectories through a low-rank parameterization may never find the attention re-organizations camouflage needs.
fastest_falsifying_experiment: Single rank-128 LoRA run on a camouflage dataset: if it already matches a known-configuration full fine-tune, the claim dies at once.
core_claim: Camouflage failures stem from grouping decisions in attention that low-rank additive updates cannot re-route, so LoRA at any practical rank plateaus far below full fine-tuning on camouflage benchmarks.
method_sketch: Rank sweep (4 to 256) vs full fine-tuning on one camouflage dataset and one ordinary-shift control, plotting gap-vs-rank saturation curves.
novelty_hook: Rank-sweep saturation analyses exist for LLMs; a task-family-specific PEFT impossibility claim in segmentation appears unmade; unverified.

title: Inter-slice adapters give 2D SAM 3D awareness

title: Where small UNets beat adapted foundation models
one_line_idea: Establish the operating regime (label count, defect size, compute) where a small from-scratch UNet beats PEFT-adapted SAM for industrial defect segmentation.

title: Few-shot adapters overfit annotator style before content
one_line_idea: Show that in few-shot SAM adaptation, adapters first learn the annotator's boundary style (tightness, smoothing, inclusion conventions) rather than domain content, and correct it with style-randomized supervision.

title: Self-distilling SAM through its own quality scores
one_line_idea: Adapt SAM to unlabeled target domains by training adapters on its own high-IoU-scored masks as pseudo-labels, with the quality head as the curator.
problem: Unlabeled target imagery is abundant, but self-training pipelines for SAM lack a principled selector and their failure conditions are uncharacterized.

title: Active learning by prompt-response inconsistency
one_line_idea: Select images for annotation where SAM's masks are most inconsistent across jittered prompts, using promptability instability as the acquisition function for PEFT.

one_line_idea: Adapt SAM to new domains using only bounding-box labels, betting that pretrained boundary competence survives domain shift and only localization/extent needs supervision.

title: One-slice test-time PEFT generalizes across a volume
one_line_idea: Fine-tune a micro-adapter on a single expert-corrected slice of a 3D scan at test time, then apply it to the remaining slices of the same patient.

title: Prune-down rank scheduling beats fixed rank at few-shot
one_line_idea: Start SAM adaptation with generous LoRA rank and progressively prune adapter singular directions during training, instead of committing to a small fixed rank.

title: Column-space-orthogonal LoRA preserves zero-shot ability
one_line_idea: Constrain LoRA updates to be orthogonal to the column space of the frozen weights they modify, hypothesizing this preserves pretrained behavior while adding target-specific directions.
problem: Unconstrained LoRA freely overwrites directions the pretrained model uses, which is the mechanistic root of zero-shot damage.
core_hypothesis: Restricting updates to the orthogonal complement of dominant pretrained weight subspaces retains most target-domain benefit while sharply reducing generic-prompt drift.
falsifiable_prediction: At matched target Dice, orthogonality-constrained LoRA shows significantly lower drift on a fixed retention suite than unconstrained LoRA, across several targets.
why_important: A drop-in constraint with no inference cost that protects the base model would be immediately adoptable by all SAM adaptation users.
why_possibly_novel: Orthogonal-update ideas circulate in continual learning; their instantiation and validation for promptable segmentation retention seems open; unverified.

community_default_belief: Regularization toward the pretrained model (e.g., weight decay to zero-update) is the way to control forgetting.

fastest_falsifying_experiment: Post-hoc project an existing trained LoRA away from dominant subspaces and measure target-Dice loss; catastrophic loss shows the constraint is unaffordable, near-zero loss supports it.

title: Null-space gradient projection for damage-free adaptation
one_line_idea: During SAM PEFT, project gradients into the null space of feature responses computed on a small generic-image reference set, so target training cannot alter behavior on the reference distribution.
problem: Existing forgetting mitigations are soft penalties with no guarantee; a hard functional constraint tailored to the frozen model's generic behavior is missing for segmentation.
core_hypothesis: Null-space projected PEFT achieves target adaptation statistically indistinguishable from unconstrained PEFT on moderate shifts while provably (to first order) fixing generic responses.

why_possibly_novel: Null-space methods exist in continual learning for classifiers; adapting the machinery to prompt-conditioned dense outputs seems technically open; unverified.

main_risk: The null space may be too small in deep layers (high effective rank of reference activations), leaving no room for adaptation.
community_default_belief: Hard constraints on adaptation are too restrictive to be practical; soft penalties suffice.
why_it_might_be_wrong: Feature matrices are famously low-rank; the null space may be far roomier than intuition suggests.

core_claim: Null-space projected PEFT achieves target adaptation statistically indistinguishable from unconstrained PEFT on moderate shifts while provably (to first order) fixing generic responses.
method_sketch: Build reference activations from a few hundred generic images, implement layer-wise null-space projection for LoRA gradients, compare against unconstrained and penalty-based baselines on two targets.

title: Adapter-strength interpolation recovers the generalist
one_line_idea: Treat the LoRA scaling coefficient as a post-hoc dial: interpolate between frozen and adapted SAM to trace the full retention-vs-target trade-off curve without retraining.
problem: Users must currently choose between the frozen generalist and the adapted specialist; whether intermediate mixtures dominate both is unquantified for segmentation.

why_possibly_novel: Weight interpolation robustness is established for classifiers; its shape for prompt-conditioned dense prediction and its use as a serving-time dial appear uncharacterized; unverified.

title: Data-free replay via generic prompts on target images
one_line_idea: Prevent forgetting without any source data by replaying frozen-SAM responses to random generic prompts on the target images themselves, as a self-generated anchor loss during PEFT.
problem: Replay-based forgetting mitigations assume access to source-distribution data, which SAM users do not have (SA-1B-scale data is impractical to replay).

falsifiable_prediction: Anchored PEFT retains substantially more zero-shot ability than unanchored PEFT at equal target Dice, despite the anchor never using non-target images.

title: Localizing forgetting: encoder vs decoder module swaps
one_line_idea: Determine whether zero-shot damage from SAM adaptation lives in the adapted encoder or decoder by systematically swapping frozen and adapted modules and measuring behavior.
problem: Forgetting in adapted SAM is reported as a scalar; nobody knows which component's changes cause it, so mitigations are untargeted.
core_hypothesis: Most zero-shot degradation is attributable to decoder-side changes, and pairing an adapted encoder with the frozen decoder recovers the bulk of generic ability.
falsifiable_prediction: In swap matrices (frozen/adapted encoder x frozen/adapted decoder), the decoder axis explains the majority of retention-suite variance across multiple adaptation runs.

why_possibly_novel: Module-swap causal analysis is common in interpretability; applying it to the forgetting question in promptable segmentation appears fresh; unverified.

why_it_might_be_wrong: The decoder is minuscule and heavily updated during adaptation, making it a plausible concentrated locus that scalar metrics hide.

method_sketch: Adapt encoder and decoder separately and jointly on two targets; evaluate all four swap combinations on target and retention suites; run variance decomposition.
novelty_hook: Module-swap causal analysis is common in interpretability; applying it to the forgetting question in promptable segmentation appears fresh; unverified.
