title: Rank, not learning rate, governs forgetting
one_line_idea: Test the claim that LoRA rank is the primary controllable determinant of zero-shot forgetting in SAM adaptation, dominating learning rate and schedule effects.
problem: Practitioners tune learning rates to be 'safe' while freely increasing rank, without evidence about which knob actually trades target gain against damage.
core_hypothesis: At matched target Dice, higher-rank/lower-LR configurations damage retention more than lower-rank/higher-LR ones, because rank sets the dimensionality of behavioral change.
falsifiable_prediction: Across a rank-LR grid with target-Dice-matched checkpoints, retention correlates strongly negatively with rank and only weakly with LR.
why_important: Identifies the honest safety knob for adaptation and corrects a possibly backwards community habit.
why_possibly_novel: Rank-vs-LR forgetting decompositions do not appear standard even in the LLM PEFT literature, let alone segmentation; unverified.

main_risk: Rank and achievable Dice are confounded; matching checkpoints on target Dice may force unequal training durations that muddy attribution.

title: Orthogonal sequential adapters approach joint multi-domain training
one_line_idea: Adapt SAM to a sequence of domains with mutually orthogonalized LoRA blocks and test how close this stays to joint multi-domain training without revisiting old data.
problem: Institutions receive domains sequentially (new scanners, new sites) but joint retraining is assumed necessary, forcing data retention that privacy rules often forbid.
core_hypothesis: Enforcing pairwise orthogonality between per-domain adapter subspaces nearly eliminates cross-domain interference, making sequential adaptation competitive with joint training.

why_possibly_novel: Orthogonal continual PEFT exists conceptually in classification; its capacity limits and behavior for promptable dense prediction remain unmapped; unverified.

novelty_hook: Orthogonal continual PEFT exists conceptually in classification; its capacity limits and behavior for promptable dense prediction remain unmapped; unverified.

title: Everything-mode collapse as the hidden cost of prompted adaptation
one_line_idea: Document and explain how adapting SAM with prompted supervision degrades its automatic mask generation (everything mode) even when prompted performance improves.
problem: Adaptation pipelines train and evaluate in prompted mode, silently shipping models whose automatic proposal ability—used by many downstream systems—may have collapsed.

title: Ordering matters: PEFT-then-distill vs distill-then-PEFT
one_line_idea: Resolve whether edge deployments should adapt the large SAM then distill to a small model, or distill first and adapt the small model, at matched total compute.
problem: Teams shipping SAM to edge devices face this ordering decision blind; the two paths plausibly differ in what domain knowledge survives compression.

title: Low-bit backbones with floating-point LoRA for SAM
one_line_idea: Quantize SAM's frozen backbone aggressively (e.g., 4-bit) and train floating-point LoRA on top, testing whether adaptation absorbs quantization damage for dense prediction.
problem: QLoRA-style recipes are proven for LLMs, but dense prediction may respond differently to backbone quantization since boundary details live in precise activations.
core_hypothesis: LoRA training on a quantized backbone compensates most quantization-induced segmentation loss, with residual damage concentrated in boundary precision rather than region accuracy.

core_claim: LoRA training on a quantized backbone compensates most quantization-induced segmentation loss, with residual damage concentrated in boundary precision rather than region accuracy.
method_sketch: On two datasets, compare {fp16, 8-bit, 4-bit} backbones each with LoRA, reporting Dice, boundary-F1, and memory footprint under one protocol.
novelty_hook: QLoRA is established in NLP; its damage decomposition (region vs boundary) for promptable segmentation seems uncharacterized; unverified.

title: Prompt-conditioned token pruning as speed-oriented PEFT
one_line_idea: Train a tiny gating adapter that drops background image tokens conditioned on the prompt, adapting SAM for speed rather than accuracy.
problem: PEFT research optimizes accuracy while inference cost, the real deployment constraint, is untouched by standard adapters.
core_hypothesis: Given a prompt, most image tokens are irrelevant to the requested mask, and a learned pruning gate can remove a large fraction with negligible accuracy loss.
falsifiable_prediction: A gating adapter prunes over half the tokens after the early blocks at under one point of Dice loss on prompted segmentation, with savings scaling with object-to-image area ratio.
why_important: Latency, not Dice, blocks SAM in interactive and video pipelines; a PEFT that buys speed changes what deployments are possible.
why_possibly_novel: Token pruning exists for classification ViTs; prompt-conditioned pruning learned as an adapter for promptable segmentation seems new; unverified.

core_claim: Given a prompt, most image tokens are irrelevant to the requested mask, and a learned pruning gate can remove a large fraction with negligible accuracy loss.
method_sketch: Insert a learned gate after block N conditioned on prompt embedding; train on one dataset with a compute penalty; report Dice-vs-FLOPs trade-off curves against uniform token merging baselines.

title: Adapter-gated early exit through encoder depth
one_line_idea: Attach lightweight exit heads at intermediate SAM encoder depths with an adapter-trained confidence gate, letting easy images skip most of the backbone.
problem: All images pay full encoder cost although many masks are easy; depth-adaptive computation has not been retrofitted to promptable segmentation.
core_hypothesis: Intermediate SAM features suffice for a large fraction of prompted masks, and a cheap gate can identify those cases reliably enough for net wall-clock savings.

core_claim: Intermediate SAM features suffice for a large fraction of prompted masks, and a cheap gate can identify those cases reliably enough for net wall-clock savings.

title: Smaller SAM variants gain more from PEFT than larger ones
one_line_idea: Test whether adaptation headroom scales inversely with backbone size, making PEFT proportionally more valuable for small/efficient SAM variants than for the largest models.
problem: PEFT papers default to the biggest backbone, leaving unknown whether conclusions transfer to the efficient variants actually deployed.

title: Adapting SAM to low-resolution inputs, mapped by object size
one_line_idea: Use PEFT to adapt SAM for reduced input resolution (e.g., 256px) and characterize exactly which object-size strata retain accuracy, yielding a resolution-selection rule.

method_sketch: PEFT SAM at three input resolutions on two datasets; report accuracy stratified by object size; test knee-point stability across domains.
novelty_hook: Resolution ablations exist informally; adaptation-assisted low-res operation with a transferable object-size law appears unformalized; unverified.
kill_risk: The knee may be blurry or domain-dependent, leaving no actionable rule.

title: Adapting the memory-read policy instead of weights in video SAM
one_line_idea: For video segmentation domains, train a tiny adapter that modulates how SAM2-style memory is read (which past frames and features to attend) rather than adapting representation weights.
problem: Video domain shifts (surgical scenes, driving) often manifest as different temporal dynamics—occlusion rates, deformation speeds—which weight-space PEFT does not directly address.
core_hypothesis: Domain-specific temporal statistics are best absorbed in the memory-attention read policy, so policy adapters outperform parameter-matched encoder LoRA on video targets.
falsifiable_prediction: Memory-read adapters beat encoder LoRA at matched parameter count on video benchmarks with distinctive temporal statistics, while tying on videos with natural-video-like dynamics.
why_important: Identifies the video-specific adaptation locus, avoiding needless perturbation of spatial representations that transfer fine.
why_possibly_novel: SAM2 adaptation is nascent; the hypothesis that temporal-domain gaps localize in memory attention seems unarticulated; unverified.
minimal_falsification_experiment: On one surgical and one driving video dataset, compare memory-attention-only adapters vs encoder LoRA vs both, measuring per-frame Dice and temporal consistency.
main_risk: Memory modules may be so entangled with spatial features that isolated policy adaptation underperforms everywhere.
community_default_belief: Video adaptation is image adaptation plus temporal smoothing; the memory mechanism is infrastructure, not an adaptation target.
why_it_might_be_wrong: Occlusion and deformation statistics differ radically across video domains, and the memory reader is the only component that models them.
fastest_falsifying_experiment: Measure memory-attention entropy distributions of frozen SAM2-style models across two video domains; identical distributions would undercut the premise that the read policy is domain-sensitive.
core_claim: Domain-specific temporal statistics are best absorbed in the memory-attention read policy, so policy adapters outperform parameter-matched encoder LoRA on video targets.
method_sketch: On one surgical and one driving video dataset, compare memory-attention-only adapters vs encoder LoRA vs both, measuring per-frame Dice and temporal consistency.
novelty_hook: SAM2 adaptation is nascent; the hypothesis that temporal-domain gaps localize in memory attention seems unarticulated; unverified.
kill_risk: Memory modules may be so entangled with spatial features that isolated policy adaptation underperforms everywhere.

title: Unstructured sparse fine-tuning vs LoRA at equal memory
one_line_idea: Compare training a small unstructured subset of SAM's weights (lottery-style masks) against LoRA at strictly matched optimizer-memory budgets for segmentation adaptation.
problem: LoRA won the PEFT mindshare partly for engineering reasons; whether structured low-rank is actually the right sparsity pattern for dense-prediction adaptation is untested.
core_hypothesis: Task-relevant adaptation directions for segmentation are better captured by a sparse subset of individual weights (especially in attention projections) than by low-rank factorizations of whole matrices.
falsifiable_prediction: At matched trainable-parameter and optimizer-state budgets, magnitude- or gradient-selected sparse fine-tuning beats LoRA on at least structure-shifted targets, with selection masks showing consistent layer patterns.
why_important: If the winning sparsity pattern is unstructured, the field's infrastructure investment in low-rank methods is leaving accuracy on the table.
why_possibly_novel: Sparse fine-tuning literature exists in NLP; a memory-matched showdown for segmentation foundation models seems missing; unverified.
minimal_falsification_experiment: Three datasets, three budgets, LoRA vs gradient-selected sparse tuning vs random-mask control, one schedule, seeds.
main_risk: Sparse-update kernels are slower in practice, making even accuracy wins operationally moot.
community_default_belief: Low-rank structure is the natural geometry of fine-tuning updates.
why_it_might_be_wrong: That geometry was validated mostly on language tasks and by convenience; full fine-tuning deltas for dense tasks have not been shown to be low-rank.
fastest_falsifying_experiment: Compute the singular-value spectrum of a full fine-tuning delta on one segmentation dataset; a heavy tail (slowly decaying spectrum) immediately challenges low-rank sufficiency.
core_claim: Task-relevant adaptation directions for segmentation are better captured by a sparse subset of individual weights (especially in attention projections) than by low-rank factorizations of whole matrices.
method_sketch: Three datasets, three budgets, LoRA vs gradient-selected sparse tuning vs random-mask control, one schedule, seeds.
novelty_hook: Sparse fine-tuning literature exists in NLP; a memory-matched showdown for segmentation foundation models seems missing; unverified.
kill_risk: Sparse-update kernels are slower in practice, making even accuracy wins operationally moot.

title: Measuring the intrinsic dimension of segmentation adaptation
one_line_idea: Estimate how many effective parameters SAM adaptation actually requires by training in random low-dimensional subspaces, across shift types and datasets.
problem: The field guesses adapter sizes with no measurement of the underlying dimensionality of the adaptation problem itself.
core_hypothesis: Segmentation domain adaptation has a low intrinsic dimension (thousands, not millions) that varies systematically with shift type, providing a principled lower bound for adapter budgets.
falsifiable_prediction: Random-subspace training reaches 90% of full fine-tuning performance at dimensions orders of magnitude below parameter count, with texture shifts requiring measurably fewer dimensions than structure shifts.
why_important: An intrinsic-dimension map would put adapter sizing on scientific footing and predict which targets are cheap or expensive before training.
why_possibly_novel: Intrinsic-dimension methodology exists for classification and NLP; its application to promptable dense prediction with a shift-type analysis appears absent; unverified.
minimal_falsification_experiment: Random-projection subspace training at 6 dimensionalities on 4 datasets spanning shift types; locate the 90%-performance dimension per dataset and correlate with shift descriptors.
main_risk: Random subspaces may be a loose bound, making measured dimensions uninformative about practical adapter design.
community_default_belief: Adapter capacity needs are an empirical matter with no measurable underlying structure.
why_it_might_be_wrong: Intrinsic-dimension results elsewhere revealed strong, task-predictive structure; there is no reason segmentation should be the exception.
fastest_falsifying_experiment: One dataset, two subspace sizes (1k and 100k): if 1k already matches 100k, dimension is trivially low and interesting; if neither approaches LoRA performance, the methodology is too loose—either outcome is informative within a day.
core_claim: Segmentation domain adaptation has a low intrinsic dimension (thousands, not millions) that varies systematically with shift type, providing a principled lower bound for adapter budgets.
method_sketch: Random-projection subspace training at 6 dimensionalities on 4 datasets spanning shift types; locate the 90%-performance dimension per dataset and correlate with shift descriptors.
novelty_hook: Intrinsic-dimension methodology exists for classification and NLP; its application to promptable dense prediction with a shift-type analysis appears absent; unverified.
kill_risk: Random subspaces may be a loose bound, making measured dimensions uninformative about practical adapter design.

title: A shared adapter subspace across medical domains
one_line_idea: Test whether LoRA updates learned independently on many medical segmentation datasets span a common low-dimensional subspace, enabling a universal 'medical basis' for future adaptation.
problem: Every medical adaptation is trained from scratch although the underlying shift (natural-to-medical imagery) is shared, suggesting massive redundancy across the community's adapters.
core_hypothesis: Independently trained medical LoRAs share dominant directions, and constraining new adaptations to the shared subspace loses little accuracy while slashing trainable dimensions.
falsifiable_prediction: Principal directions extracted from adapters trained on N medical datasets transfer to unseen medical datasets: training only coefficients in that basis reaches near-full LoRA performance at a tiny dimension.
why_important: A validated shared basis would make medical SAM adaptation a coefficients-only problem—faster, cheaper, and more robust at low labels.
why_possibly_novel: Cross-task adapter subspace analyses exist in NLP; a medical-imaging shared-basis claim for segmentation is concrete and untested; unverified.
minimal_falsification_experiment: Train LoRAs on 6-8 public medical datasets, compute cross-adapter subspace overlap, then adapt to two held-out datasets restricted to the shared basis vs free LoRA.
main_risk: Modality diversity within 'medical' (CT vs ultrasound vs pathology) may fragment the subspace into modality islands.
community_default_belief: Each dataset's adaptation is idiosyncratic; adapters are not expected to share structure across datasets.
why_it_might_be_wrong: All medical targets share the same source model and overlapping shift causes, which should imprint common structure on the updates.
fastest_falsifying_experiment: Compute subspace principal angles between two existing medical LoRAs; near-orthogonality between even same-modality adapters would immediately undermine the shared-basis premise.
core_claim: Independently trained medical LoRAs share dominant directions, and constraining new adaptations to the shared subspace loses little accuracy while slashing trainable dimensions.
method_sketch: Train LoRAs on 6-8 public medical datasets, compute cross-adapter subspace overlap, then adapt to two held-out datasets restricted to the shared basis vs free LoRA.
novelty_hook: Cross-task adapter subspace analyses exist in NLP; a medical-imaging shared-basis claim for segmentation is concrete and untested; unverified.
