title: Feature-statistics matching as a train-free adaptation baseline
one_line_idea: Adapt SAM without gradients by re-normalizing target-domain features to match source-domain feature statistics (mean/covariance per layer), testing how much of PEFT's gain is mere re-statistics.
problem: Nobody knows what fraction of learned adaptation is explained by simple distribution matching, so gradient-based PEFT gets credit it may not deserve.
core_hypothesis: A significant fraction of LoRA's gain on appearance-shifted targets is reproduced by closed-form feature whitening-recoloring toward source statistics computed from unlabeled data.
falsifiable_prediction: Train-free statistics matching recovers a substantial share of the frozen-to-LoRA gap on appearance shifts and nearly none on structure shifts, with the recovered share predictable from feature-distribution distances.
why_important: Establishes an honest zero-training baseline every adaptation paper should report, and dissects what adaptation is.
why_possibly_novel: AdaBN-style ideas are classic for batch-norm networks; their formulation for LayerNorm ViT segmentation backbones as an analysis instrument seems underdeveloped; unverified.
minimal_falsification_experiment: Implement per-layer whitening-recoloring from unlabeled target and source statistics; evaluate against frozen and LoRA-adapted SAM on datasets spanning shift types.
main_risk: LayerNorm architectures may already neutralize the first-order statistics the method manipulates, leaving nothing to gain.
community_default_belief: Adaptation gains reflect learned task- and domain-specific structure requiring optimization.
why_it_might_be_wrong: In classifiers, large adaptation effects have repeatedly reduced to normalization statistics; segmentation has never run that control.
fastest_falsifying_experiment: Match only per-channel means at three depths on one dataset; any measurable Dice movement in an afternoon justifies the full study, none refutes the premise for that dataset.
core_claim: A significant fraction of LoRA's gain on appearance-shifted targets is reproduced by closed-form feature whitening-recoloring toward source statistics computed from unlabeled data.
method_sketch: Implement per-layer whitening-recoloring from unlabeled target and source statistics; evaluate against frozen and LoRA-adapted SAM on datasets spanning shift types.
novelty_hook: AdaBN-style ideas are classic for batch-norm networks; their formulation for LayerNorm ViT segmentation backbones as an analysis instrument seems underdeveloped; unverified.
kill_risk: LayerNorm architectures may already neutralize the first-order statistics the method manipulates, leaving nothing to gain.

title: Mode connectivity of independently trained SAM adapters
one_line_idea: Test whether two LoRAs trained on the same target from different seeds are linearly connected (low-loss interpolation path) in adapter space, and exploit connectivity for adapter averaging.
problem: Basic loss-landscape geometry of segmentation PEFT is unknown, blocking principled use of adapter merging, averaging, and ensembling.
core_hypothesis: Same-task adapters live in a connected low-loss basin (after accounting for factorization symmetry), so weight-averaged adapters match or beat individual ones.
falsifiable_prediction: Linear interpolation between seed-different adapters shows no loss barrier after aligning factorizations, and the midpoint adapter equals or exceeds endpoint Dice on held-out data.
why_important: Connectivity legitimizes cheap adapter soups—free accuracy and robustness from runs teams already perform.
why_possibly_novel: Mode connectivity is studied for full networks in classification; the adapter-subspace version for dense prediction seems unexamined; unverified.
minimal_falsification_experiment: Train 3 seeds on each of two datasets, align low-rank factors (e.g., via orthogonal Procrustes), sweep interpolations, measure barriers and midpoint quality.
main_risk: LoRA's factorization non-identifiability may make alignment itself the hard problem, confounding the geometry question.
community_default_belief: Averaging independently trained networks or modules requires special training constraints to work.
why_it_might_be_wrong: Adapters are tiny perturbations around a shared frozen anchor—the friendliest known setting for connectivity, unlike the from-scratch settings the caution came from.
fastest_falsifying_experiment: Average two seed adapters naively (no alignment) on one dataset; if the average already works, connectivity is strongly suggested in an hour; a collapse motivates only the aligned test before giving up.
core_claim: Same-task adapters live in a connected low-loss basin (after accounting for factorization symmetry), so weight-averaged adapters match or beat individual ones.
method_sketch: Train 3 seeds on each of two datasets, align low-rank factors (e.g., via orthogonal Procrustes), sweep interpolations, measure barriers and midpoint quality.
novelty_hook: Mode connectivity is studied for full networks in classification; the adapter-subspace version for dense prediction seems unexamined; unverified.
kill_risk: LoRA's factorization non-identifiability may make alignment itself the hard problem, confounding the geometry question.

title: First-epoch curves predict final adaptation quality
one_line_idea: Build a predictor of final adapted-SAM performance from first-epoch training signals (loss slope, gradient noise scale, prompt-consistency trend), enabling early abandonment of doomed configurations.
problem: PEFT configuration searches waste most compute on runs whose failure was visible early, but no validated early-stopping predictor exists for segmentation adaptation.
core_hypothesis: Final target Dice is predictable from first-epoch dynamics with enough fidelity to safely prune the bottom half of a configuration sweep.
falsifiable_prediction: A predictor trained on logged sweeps ranks final performance of unseen configurations with high rank-correlation, and pruning its bottom half loses the true best configuration rarely.
why_important: Halving sweep compute changes what small labs can afford to explore, and the predictor's features reveal what early dynamics matter.
why_possibly_novel: Learning-curve extrapolation exists for architecture search; a PEFT-specific, segmentation-specific instantiation with prompt-consistency features seems new; unverified.
minimal_falsification_experiment: Log rich first-epoch telemetry across a 50-configuration sweep on two datasets; fit and cross-validate the predictor; measure pruning regret.
main_risk: Early dynamics may be schedule-dominated, making the predictor a schedule detector rather than a quality forecaster.
community_default_belief: Fine-tuning outcomes are noisy and only distinguishable after substantial training.
why_it_might_be_wrong: PEFT's tiny parameter space makes optimization unusually well-behaved, plausibly exposing outcome-relevant signal from the first hundreds of steps.
fastest_falsifying_experiment: On an existing sweep's logs, correlate epoch-1 loss with final Dice; near-zero correlation across configurations ends the idea without new training.
core_claim: Final target Dice is predictable from first-epoch dynamics with enough fidelity to safely prune the bottom half of a configuration sweep.
method_sketch: Log rich first-epoch telemetry across a 50-configuration sweep on two datasets; fit and cross-validate the predictor; measure pruning regret.
novelty_hook: Learning-curve extrapolation exists for architecture search; a PEFT-specific, segmentation-specific instantiation with prompt-consistency features seems new; unverified.
kill_risk: Early dynamics may be schedule-dominated, making the predictor a schedule detector rather than a quality forecaster.

title: Attention drift, not feature drift, marks where adaptation is needed
one_line_idea: Compare attention-pattern divergence vs feature-magnitude divergence between source and target imagery as competing predictors of which SAM layers need adapters.
problem: Layer-selection heuristics use feature-distribution distances, implicitly assuming feature drift is the actionable signal; attention structure might be the truer indicator.
core_hypothesis: Layers whose attention maps reorganize under domain shift are the layers where adapters yield the most gain, and attention drift predicts this better than feature drift.
falsifiable_prediction: Across datasets, per-layer adapter value (measured by leave-one-layer-in training) correlates more strongly with attention-map divergence than with feature-statistic divergence.
why_important: Establishes the right diagnostic quantity for placement decisions and illuminates what domain shift does inside ViTs mechanistically.
why_possibly_novel: Both divergences are measurable with known tools; their head-to-head comparison as placement predictors seems unrun; unverified.
minimal_falsification_experiment: Compute both divergence profiles on 4 datasets; run single-layer adapter trainings to get ground-truth per-layer value; compare predictor correlations.
main_risk: Single-layer adapter value may be a poor proxy for value within multi-layer configurations due to interactions.
community_default_belief: Feature-distribution shift is the operative quantity for adaptation decisions.
why_it_might_be_wrong: Feature statistics can drift harmlessly under LayerNorm while attention reorganization directly changes grouping—the computation segmentation depends on.
fastest_falsifying_experiment: On one dataset, check whether the layer with maximal attention drift differs at all from the layer with maximal feature drift; identical profiles would make the comparison moot.
core_claim: Layers whose attention maps reorganize under domain shift are the layers where adapters yield the most gain, and attention drift predicts this better than feature drift.
method_sketch: Compute both divergence profiles on 4 datasets; run single-layer adapter trainings to get ground-truth per-layer value; compare predictor correlations.
novelty_hook: Both divergences are measurable with known tools; their head-to-head comparison as placement predictors seems unrun; unverified.
kill_risk: Single-layer adapter value may be a poor proxy for value within multi-layer configurations due to interactions.

title: Adapters learn prompt-independent corrections
one_line_idea: Test whether the corrections encoder-side adapters learn are effectively independent of the prompt, implying adaptation is an image-processing change that could be moved to cheaper input-side modules.
problem: It is unknown whether learned adaptation interacts with the prompt pathway or merely re-processes the image, a distinction that dictates where adapters belong architecturally.
core_hypothesis: Encoder adapter contributions to the final mask vary little across prompts for a fixed image, showing adaptation is prompt-agnostic image correction.
falsifiable_prediction: Ablating adapter outputs while varying prompts shows near-constant adapter effect per image; and an input-side module distilled from the adapter reproduces most of its gain.
why_important: If adaptation is prompt-agnostic, the field can move it wholesale to input-space modules that are shareable, inspectable, and backbone-version-proof.
why_possibly_novel: Nobody appears to have decomposed adapter effects along the prompt dimension for promptable models; unverified.
minimal_falsification_experiment: For adapted models on two datasets, measure variance of adapter-induced mask changes across prompt sets per image; attempt distillation of the adapter into an input-space network.
main_risk: The decomposition may be scale-dependent (prompt-agnostic early, prompt-dependent late), complicating a clean verdict.
community_default_belief: Adapters learn task-and-prompt-entangled corrections that must live inside the network.
why_it_might_be_wrong: Encoder adapters physically cannot see the prompt in SAM's architecture (prompts enter at the decoder), so prompt-dependence of their learned function is at best indirect—yet nobody has quantified how prompt-agnostic their effect on final masks is.
fastest_falsifying_experiment: One adapted checkpoint, 20 images, 10 prompts each: compute variance of adapter effect across prompts; high variance immediately falsifies prompt-agnosticism.
core_claim: Encoder adapter contributions to the final mask vary little across prompts for a fixed image, showing adaptation is prompt-agnostic image correction.
method_sketch: For adapted models on two datasets, measure variance of adapter-induced mask changes across prompt sets per image; attempt distillation of the adapter into an input-space network.
novelty_hook: Nobody appears to have decomposed adapter effects along the prompt dimension for promptable models; unverified.
kill_risk: The decomposition may be scale-dependent (prompt-agnostic early, prompt-dependent late), complicating a clean verdict.

title: Allocated rank is mostly wasted: effective-rank collapse
one_line_idea: Measure the effective rank of trained SAM adapters across allocated ranks, testing whether learned updates collapse to a few directions regardless of budget.
problem: Rank is treated as meaningful capacity, but if optimization concentrates updates in a handful of directions, most allocated rank is dead weight and rank sweeps are theater.
core_hypothesis: Trained adapters exhibit effective rank far below allocated rank (spectral mass concentrated in the top 2-4 directions), stable across allocations from 8 to 128.
falsifiable_prediction: Post-hoc truncation of trained adapters to their top-4 directions loses almost no target Dice across datasets and allocated ranks, while truncation to rank-1 shows task-dependent loss.
why_important: Would redirect the field from rank tuning toward direction quality, and enable aggressive post-hoc adapter compression for storage and serving.
why_possibly_novel: Spectral analyses of LLM LoRAs exist informally; a systematic segmentation-focused study connecting collapse to truncation safety appears missing; unverified.
minimal_falsification_experiment: Train adapters at 4 allocated ranks on 3 datasets; compute spectra; evaluate truncated versions at multiple cut points.
main_risk: Collapse may itself be an artifact of standard initialization and LR choices, limiting generality.
community_default_belief: Higher allocated rank means more usable adaptation capacity.
why_it_might_be_wrong: Gradient dynamics on factorized parameterizations are known to bias toward low-rank solutions, so allocation and utilization can diverge wildly.
fastest_falsifying_experiment: Compute the singular spectrum of any single existing trained adapter; a flat spectrum on the first checkpoint examined challenges collapse immediately.
core_claim: Trained adapters exhibit effective rank far below allocated rank (spectral mass concentrated in the top 2-4 directions), stable across allocations from 8 to 128.
method_sketch: Train adapters at 4 allocated ranks on 3 datasets; compute spectra; evaluate truncated versions at multiple cut points.
novelty_hook: Spectral analyses of LLM LoRAs exist informally; a systematic segmentation-focused study connecting collapse to truncation safety appears missing; unverified.
kill_risk: Collapse may itself be an artifact of standard initialization and LR choices, limiting generality.

title: PEFT gains live at boundaries: a trimap decomposition
one_line_idea: Decompose every SAM adaptation gain into boundary-band vs interior contributions, testing whether PEFT mostly refines borders while interiors were already correct.
problem: Dice improvements are reported as scalars, hiding whether adaptation fixes object discovery, interior filling, or only boundary placement—each implying different methods.
core_hypothesis: For moderate shifts, a large majority of PEFT's Dice gain comes from a thin boundary band, implying boundary-specialized adapters and losses would be more efficient than whole-image adaptation.
falsifiable_prediction: Trimap analysis across recipes and datasets attributes most gain to boundary bands on moderate shifts, and boundary-weighted training recovers standard-training gains at reduced compute or parameters.
why_important: Changes what adaptation methods should optimize and how papers should report, replacing scalar Dice deltas with located improvements.
why_possibly_novel: Trimap evaluation is standard in matting/segmentation evaluation; using it to dissect and then redesign PEFT appears new; unverified.
minimal_falsification_experiment: Re-evaluate several adaptation runs with band-stratified metrics on 4 datasets; then train boundary-loss-weighted adapters and compare efficiency.
main_risk: On severe shifts gains may be discovery-dominated, restricting the claim to a shift-severity regime that must be delineated.
community_default_belief: Adaptation gains reflect broadly improved features rather than a spatially localized fix.
why_it_might_be_wrong: Frozen SAM typically finds the right object but misplaces extents under moderate shift, so the residual error—and hence the gain—must be geometrically concentrated.
fastest_falsifying_experiment: Band-stratify the improvement of one existing adapted checkpoint; interior-dominated gains on the first dataset immediately bound the claim.
core_claim: For moderate shifts, a large majority of PEFT's Dice gain comes from a thin boundary band, implying boundary-specialized adapters and losses would be more efficient than whole-image adaptation.
method_sketch: Re-evaluate several adaptation runs with band-stratified metrics on 4 datasets; then train boundary-loss-weighted adapters and compare efficiency.
novelty_hook: Trimap evaluation is standard in matting/segmentation evaluation; using it to dissect and then redesign PEFT appears new; unverified.
kill_risk: On severe shifts gains may be discovery-dominated, restricting the claim to a shift-severity regime that must be delineated.

title: Loss choice erases placement effects in SAM PEFT
one_line_idea: Run a factorial study of adapter placement x loss function, testing whether boundary-aware losses eliminate the performance differences between placement strategies.
problem: Placement papers and loss papers evolve separately; if strong losses make placement irrelevant, much placement research is optimizing a vanishing effect.
core_hypothesis: With boundary- and topology-aware losses, performance variance across adapter placements shrinks dramatically, because good gradients find adaptation capacity wherever it sits.
falsifiable_prediction: In a placement-by-loss factorial on multiple datasets, the placement main effect and its share of variance drop severalfold when moving from plain Dice/CE losses to boundary-aware losses.
why_important: Would re-prioritize the field's attention from architecture placement toward training signals, or, if falsified, put placement research on firmer ground.
why_possibly_novel: Factorial placement-loss interaction studies appear absent from the SAM adaptation literature; unverified.
minimal_falsification_experiment: 3 placements x 3 losses x 3 datasets with seeds; two-way ANOVA on final metrics; report interaction structure.
main_risk: Compute cost of the full factorial; effect sizes may demand more seeds than budgeted.
community_default_belief: Placement and loss are independent design choices whose benefits add.
why_it_might_be_wrong: Both mechanisms plausibly compensate for the same underfitting failure, making them substitutes rather than complements.
fastest_falsifying_experiment: One dataset, 2x2 corner of the factorial: if the placement gap is identical under both losses, the interaction hypothesis loses its motivating case cheaply.
core_claim: With boundary- and topology-aware losses, performance variance across adapter placements shrinks dramatically, because good gradients find adaptation capacity wherever it sits.
method_sketch: 3 placements x 3 losses x 3 datasets with seeds; two-way ANOVA on final metrics; report interaction structure.
novelty_hook: Factorial placement-loss interaction studies appear absent from the SAM adaptation literature; unverified.
kill_risk: Compute cost of the full factorial; effect sizes may demand more seeds than budgeted.

title: Does task arithmetic work for segmentation adapters?
one_line_idea: Test additive composition of SAM LoRAs—combining a modality adapter with an anatomy adapter trained separately—to synthesize adaptation for their unseen intersection.
problem: Every modality-task pair is adapted from scratch; if adapters composed additively, the community's library of single-purpose adapters would cover combinatorial ground for free.
core_hypothesis: Adapter arithmetic (weighted sums of LoRA deltas) transfers meaningfully to prompt-conditioned dense prediction: composed adapters beat both parents and the frozen model on intersection tasks.
falsifiable_prediction: On an intersection dataset (e.g., a structure type in a modality where neither parent trained on the pair), the composed adapter recovers a substantial fraction of the gain of an oracle adapter trained directly on the pair.
why_important: Composability turns N adapters into N-squared capabilities and would reshape how adaptation libraries are built and shared.
why_possibly_novel: Task arithmetic is documented for classification and generation; its validity for promptable segmentation adapters is unknown; unverified.
minimal_falsification_experiment: Train parent adapters on disjoint axes (modality-only and structure-only data), compose with coefficient sweeps, evaluate on the held-out intersection vs oracle and frozen baselines.
main_risk: Dense-prediction adapters may interfere destructively, producing mask artifacts rather than graceful composition.
community_default_belief: Weight-space arithmetic is a curiosity that breaks outside simple classification settings.
why_it_might_be_wrong: Low-rank deltas around a shared frozen anchor are the best-conditioned case for linearity assumptions; segmentation has simply not been tested.
fastest_falsifying_experiment: Compose any two existing adapters and run everything-mode on 20 images; catastrophic artifacts falsify composability immediately, clean masks justify the full study.
core_claim: Adapter arithmetic (weighted sums of LoRA deltas) transfers meaningfully to prompt-conditioned dense prediction: composed adapters beat both parents and the frozen model on intersection tasks.
method_sketch: Train parent adapters on disjoint axes (modality-only and structure-only data), compose with coefficient sweeps, evaluate on the held-out intersection vs oracle and frozen baselines.
novelty_hook: Task arithmetic is documented for classification and generation; its validity for promptable segmentation adapters is unknown; unverified.
kill_risk: Dense-prediction adapters may interfere destructively, producing mask artifacts rather than graceful composition.

title: Train-free routing over an adapter library
one_line_idea: Serve many domain adapters behind a single frozen SAM using a training-free router that picks the adapter whose training-data feature statistics best match the incoming image.
problem: Multi-domain SAM services must decide which adapter to apply per request; learned routers add training and maintenance burden that a statistics-based nearest-neighbor rule might avoid.
core_hypothesis: Frozen-SAM feature statistics identify the source domain of an image reliably enough that nearest-centroid routing achieves near-oracle adapter selection.
falsifiable_prediction: On a pooled multi-domain test stream, nearest-centroid routing selects the oracle-best adapter for the vast majority of images and loses only marginal Dice versus oracle routing.
why_important: Zero-training routing makes adapter libraries plug-and-play: adding a domain requires only computing its centroid.
why_possibly_novel: Mixture-of-adapters with learned routers exists; a deliberately training-free statistics router evaluated against oracle routing for segmentation seems unexamined; unverified.
minimal_falsification_experiment: Build a 6-adapter library, compute per-domain feature centroids, route a mixed test stream, compare against oracle, random, and single-best-adapter baselines.
main_risk: Images near domain boundaries (e.g., two ultrasound datasets) may route incorrectly exactly where adapter choice matters most.
community_default_belief: Reliable routing requires a learned gating network trained on all domains jointly.
why_it_might_be_wrong: Domain identity is among the easiest signals in deep features—far easier than the segmentation task itself—so learning a router may be overkill.
fastest_falsifying_experiment: Cluster frozen-SAM pooled features of images from 6 datasets; poor cluster purity in a confusion matrix falsifies routability in an hour.
core_claim: Frozen-SAM feature statistics identify the source domain of an image reliably enough that nearest-centroid routing achieves near-oracle adapter selection.
method_sketch: Build a 6-adapter library, compute per-domain feature centroids, route a mixed test stream, compare against oracle, random, and single-best-adapter baselines.
novelty_hook: Mixture-of-adapters with learned routers exists; a deliberately training-free statistics router evaluated against oracle routing for segmentation seems unexamined; unverified.
kill_risk: Images near domain boundaries (e.g., two ultrasound datasets) may route incorrectly exactly where adapter choice matters most.

title: Superposition capacity: one adapter, many organs
one_line_idea: Measure how many distinct segmentation tasks (organs/structures) a single fixed-rank SAM adapter can hold before interference degrades them, mapping PEFT's superposition capacity.
problem: Teams choose between per-task adapters and one shared adapter with no quantitative model of when sharing starts to hurt.
core_hypothesis: Task capacity of an adapter scales roughly linearly with rank up to a knee, beyond which adding tasks causes abrupt mutual interference rather than graceful decay.
falsifiable_prediction: Training one adapter on k tasks for increasing k at fixed rank shows a capacity knee whose location scales predictably with rank, and per-task Dice beyond the knee drops sharply rather than smoothly.
why_important: A capacity law would let practitioners provision adapters like memory—rank chosen from task count—replacing guesswork in multi-task deployments.
why_possibly_novel: Multi-task PEFT exists; a quantitative capacity-vs-rank law with knee characterization for segmentation seems unmeasured; unverified.
minimal_falsification_experiment: Fixed rank, train adapters on nested task sets (k=1..12 structures) from a multi-organ dataset; repeat at three ranks; plot per-task performance vs k.
main_risk: Task relatedness confounds capacity: similar organs may share capacity while dissimilar ones collide early, blurring the knee.
community_default_belief: One adapter per task is safest; shared adapters degrade gradually and unpredictably.
why_it_might_be_wrong: Superposition studies in other networks show structured, predictable capacity limits, suggesting the degradation is lawful rather than unpredictable.
fastest_falsifying_experiment: Rank-8 adapter on 2 vs 8 organs: if per-organ Dice is identical in both, capacity limits are far away and the knee (if any) is impractical to map; if 8 collapses, the law is worth mapping.
core_claim: Task capacity of an adapter scales roughly linearly with rank up to a knee, beyond which adding tasks causes abrupt mutual interference rather than graceful decay.
method_sketch: Fixed rank, train adapters on nested task sets (k=1..12 structures) from a multi-organ dataset; repeat at three ranks; plot per-task performance vs k.
novelty_hook: Multi-task PEFT exists; a quantitative capacity-vs-rank law with knee characterization for segmentation seems unmeasured; unverified.
kill_risk: Task relatedness confounds capacity: similar organs may share capacity while dissimilar ones collide early, blurring the knee.

title: When federated averaging of segmentation LoRAs fails
one_line_idea: Characterize the failure conditions of naive FedAvg over SAM LoRAs across hospitals and test simple subspace-alignment fixes.
problem: Federated PEFT is proposed for privacy-bound medical adaptation, but averaging low-rank factors is mathematically dubious (factor misalignment) and its practical failure modes are unmapped for segmentation.
core_hypothesis: Naive averaging of LoRA factors degrades sharply as client domains diverge, and aligning factor subspaces before averaging recovers most of the loss without extra communication.
falsifiable_prediction: In simulated multi-site training with controlled site heterogeneity, naive FedAvg underperforms local adapters beyond a heterogeneity threshold, while Procrustes-aligned averaging stays close to centralized training much longer.
why_important: Federated adaptation is the only viable path for many clinical consortia; knowing when it silently fails prevents deployed regressions.
why_possibly_novel: Federated LoRA papers exist for LLMs; heterogeneity-threshold analysis with alignment fixes for dense medical prediction appears open; unverified.
minimal_falsification_experiment: Partition public multi-site datasets by site; run naive, aligned, and local-only protocols across heterogeneity levels; report per-site and global Dice.
main_risk: Public multi-site segmentation data may not span enough heterogeneity to locate the failure threshold convincingly.
community_default_belief: FedAvg extends to adapter parameters as straightforwardly as to full weights.
why_it_might_be_wrong: Averaging factorized matrices averages the wrong object: identical functions can have orthogonal factorizations that cancel under averaging.
fastest_falsifying_experiment: Average two same-task different-seed LoRAs naively and evaluate; if even the homogeneous case degrades, the misalignment pathology is confirmed within an hour.
core_claim: Naive averaging of LoRA factors degrades sharply as client domains diverge, and aligning factor subspaces before averaging recovers most of the loss without extra communication.
method_sketch: Partition public multi-site datasets by site; run naive, aligned, and local-only protocols across heterogeneity levels; report per-site and global Dice.
novelty_hook: Federated LoRA papers exist for LLMs; heterogeneity-threshold analysis with alignment fixes for dense medical prediction appears open; unverified.
kill_risk: Public multi-site segmentation data may not span enough heterogeneity to locate the failure threshold convincingly.

title: Adapter retrieval instead of adapter training
one_line_idea: For a new unlabeled target domain, retrieve the best-matching adapter from a public zoo by comparing feature statistics, deploying with zero target training.
problem: Many practitioners cannot train at all (no labels, no GPUs), but the community collectively owns hundreds of trained adapters that might already cover their domain.
core_hypothesis: Domain similarity computed from frozen-SAM features predicts cross-domain adapter transfer quality well enough that retrieved adapters beat the frozen model on most new targets.
falsifiable_prediction: Across held-out target datasets, the feature-similarity-retrieved adapter improves over frozen SAM in the majority of cases, and retrieval ranking correlates strongly with actual transfer ranking.
why_important: Would establish adapter reuse as a legitimate deployment mode and motivate standardized adapter sharing with feature-statistics metadata.
why_possibly_novel: Model zoos with transferability estimation exist for full models; statistics-indexed retrieval over segmentation adapter libraries seems unbuilt; unverified.
minimal_falsification_experiment: Train a 10-adapter zoo, hold out 5 target datasets, compare retrieved-adapter vs frozen vs oracle-selected adapter, and correlate similarity scores with transfer outcomes.
main_risk: Adapter transfer may be brittle: near-domain adapters could actively hurt via convention mismatches, making retrieval worse than frozen defaults.
community_default_belief: Adapters are dataset-specific artifacts that do not transfer usefully to other datasets.
why_it_might_be_wrong: Much of what adapters learn is shared shift structure (modality statistics), which neighboring domains need too; the belief has never been tested at zoo scale.
fastest_falsifying_experiment: Apply one ultrasound-trained adapter to a different ultrasound dataset: if it underperforms frozen SAM there, near-domain transfer already fails in its easiest case.
core_claim: Domain similarity computed from frozen-SAM features predicts cross-domain adapter transfer quality well enough that retrieved adapters beat the frozen model on most new targets.
method_sketch: Train a 10-adapter zoo, hold out 5 target datasets, compare retrieved-adapter vs frozen vs oracle-selected adapter, and correlate similarity scores with transfer outcomes.
novelty_hook: Model zoos with transferability estimation exist for full models; statistics-indexed retrieval over segmentation adapter libraries seems unbuilt; unverified.
kill_risk: Adapter transfer may be brittle: near-domain adapters could actively hurt via convention mismatches, making retrieval worse than frozen defaults.

title: Zero-interference continual adaptation by rank growth
one_line_idea: Support unbounded domain sequences by allocating each new domain a fresh rank block constrained orthogonal to all previous blocks, with first-order zero-interference by construction.
problem: Continual SAM deployment (new scanners, seasons, sites) needs adaptation that provably never damages previous domains, which penalty-based methods cannot guarantee.
core_hypothesis: Orthogonal rank-block growth achieves per-domain performance close to individually trained adapters while old-domain performance stays exactly frozen-stable, up to many domains before capacity saturates.
falsifiable_prediction: Over a 10-domain sequence, old-domain Dice under rank growth stays within noise of its value at learning time, while unconstrained sequential tuning shows measurable regression, at comparable final per-domain accuracy.
why_important: A no-regression guarantee is what regulated deployments (clinical, industrial QA) actually require to permit continual updates.
why_possibly_novel: Orthogonal expansion appears in continual learning theory; a practical instantiation with guarantees for promptable segmentation seems missing; unverified.
minimal_falsification_experiment: Implement per-domain orthogonal rank blocks with a domain-routing switch; run a 10-domain sequence against sequential fine-tuning and per-domain adapters; audit old-domain drift.
main_risk: Nonlinearity makes parameter-space orthogonality only a first-order guarantee; higher-order interference could still leak.
community_default_belief: Continual learning inevitably trades stability against plasticity; guarantees require freezing everything.
why_it_might_be_wrong: With a frozen backbone and additive orthogonal updates gated per domain, the trade-off may be sidestepped rather than balanced.
fastest_falsifying_experiment: Two-domain version: measure domain-1 drift after domain-2 training with gated orthogonal blocks; any drift beyond numerical noise falsifies the mechanism at once.
core_claim: Orthogonal rank-block growth achieves per-domain performance close to individually trained adapters while old-domain performance stays exactly frozen-stable, up to many domains before capacity saturates.
method_sketch: Implement per-domain orthogonal rank blocks with a domain-routing switch; run a 10-domain sequence against sequential fine-tuning and per-domain adapters; audit old-domain drift.
novelty_hook: Orthogonal expansion appears in continual learning theory; a practical instantiation with guarantees for promptable segmentation seems missing; unverified.
kill_risk: Nonlinearity makes parameter-space orthogonality only a first-order guarantee; higher-order interference could still leak.

title: Split personalization: shared adapters, private prompts
one_line_idea: In multi-institution settings, share a jointly trained LoRA while each site keeps small private learned prompt tokens, splitting adaptation into a common representation part and a local convention part.
problem: Sites differ both in imaging (shareable structure) and in local annotation conventions (private, idiosyncratic), but current federated schemes entangle the two in one artifact.
core_hypothesis: The shared-LoRA-plus-private-prompt decomposition matches fully local adaptation per site while communicating only the shared part, because conventions are expressible in prompt space.
falsifiable_prediction: On multi-site data with convention differences, the split scheme reaches per-site accuracy within noise of per-site full adapters, while a shared-everything scheme shows systematic per-site bias.
why_important: Cleanly separates what should be pooled from what should stay local—both a systems win (less communication) and a privacy win.
why_possibly_novel: Personalization layers exist in federated learning; mapping the personalization axis onto SAM's prompt space specifically seems fresh; unverified.
minimal_falsification_experiment: Simulate 4 sites with re-annotated conventions; compare split scheme vs shared-everything vs local-everything on per-site test sets.
main_risk: Convention differences may exceed prompt-space expressiveness, forcing private LoRA components and diluting the claim.
community_default_belief: Personalization requires per-site weight components; prompts are not a personalization mechanism.
why_it_might_be_wrong: Boundary conventions are output-style choices, which is exactly the kind of low-dimensional steering prompt tokens have shown they can carry.
fastest_falsifying_experiment: Train private prompt tokens alone (no shared LoRA) to absorb a convention difference between two annotation styles on one dataset; failure there kills the decomposition's key assumption.
core_claim: The shared-LoRA-plus-private-prompt decomposition matches fully local adaptation per site while communicating only the shared part, because conventions are expressible in prompt space.
method_sketch: Simulate 4 sites with re-annotated conventions; compare split scheme vs shared-everything vs local-everything on per-site test sets.
novelty_hook: Personalization layers exist in federated learning; mapping the personalization axis onto SAM's prompt space specifically seems fresh; unverified.
kill_risk: Convention differences may exceed prompt-space expressiveness, forcing private LoRA components and diluting the claim.

title: Transplanting adapters across SAM backbone sizes
one_line_idea: Transfer a LoRA trained on a small SAM variant to a larger variant (or vice versa) via cross-model subspace alignment, avoiding retraining when backbones are swapped.
problem: Organizations upgrade or downgrade backbones routinely, and every swap currently invalidates all trained adapters.
core_hypothesis: Adapter updates encode backbone-agnostic domain corrections in a subspace that can be mapped between differently sized encoders with a cheap linear alignment learned from paired activations on unlabeled images.
falsifiable_prediction: Aligned-transplanted adapters recover a large fraction of natively trained adapter gains on the destination backbone, dramatically beating random and unaligned transplant controls.
why_important: Backbone-portable adapters would decouple adaptation investment from model-version churn, an unglamorous but expensive real-world pain.
why_possibly_novel: Cross-model stitching literature exists for representations; porting trained PEFT artifacts across backbone scales seems largely untried; unverified.
minimal_falsification_experiment: Learn linear maps between small and large SAM activation spaces from unlabeled images; transplant three domain adapters each way; evaluate against native training.
main_risk: Layer correspondence between different depths is ambiguous, and the needed correction may be expressed at non-matching depths.
community_default_belief: Adapters are strictly tied to the exact weights they were trained on.
why_it_might_be_wrong: Representational similarity findings show strong cross-model alignment of features, and adapters act on those features rather than on arbitrary coordinates.
fastest_falsifying_experiment: Measure linear predictability between small-SAM and large-SAM features on shared images; poor alignment at every depth pair ends the idea without transplant experiments.
core_claim: Adapter updates encode backbone-agnostic domain corrections in a subspace that can be mapped between differently sized encoders with a cheap linear alignment learned from paired activations on unlabeled images.
method_sketch: Learn linear maps between small and large SAM activation spaces from unlabeled images; transplant three domain adapters each way; evaluate against native training.
novelty_hook: Cross-model stitching literature exists for representations; porting trained PEFT artifacts across backbone scales seems largely untried; unverified.
kill_risk: Layer correspondence between different depths is ambiguous, and the needed correction may be expressed at non-matching depths.

title: Compressing an adapter library into one hypernetwork
one_line_idea: Distill a library of per-domain SAM adapters into a single small hypernetwork that generates adapter weights from a domain embedding, enabling continuous interpolation between domains.
problem: Adapter libraries grow linearly with domains, and discrete libraries cannot serve intermediate or blended domains (e.g., a scanner between two calibrations).
core_hypothesis: Trained adapters occupy a smooth low-dimensional manifold that a hypernetwork can parameterize, making generated adapters match stored ones and interpolations meaningful.
falsifiable_prediction: Hypernetwork-generated adapters match stored adapters within a small Dice margin on their own domains, and interpolated embeddings outperform both endpoint adapters on genuinely intermediate test data.
why_important: Turns adapter management from artifact storage into a compact generative model, and tests whether domain adaptation space is continuous.
why_possibly_novel: Hypernetworks for PEFT exist in NLP research; the manifold-continuity claim and intermediate-domain evaluation for segmentation appear new; unverified.
minimal_falsification_experiment: Train 10 domain adapters, fit a hypernetwork on 8, test reconstruction on 2 held-out; evaluate interpolated adapters on constructed intermediate-domain data (e.g., graded corruption levels).
main_risk: Held-out reconstruction may fail because 8 domains undersample the manifold, requiring an impractically large library.
community_default_belief: Adapters are independent point solutions; the space between them has no meaning.
why_it_might_be_wrong: Domains themselves vary continuously (dose, gain, stain concentration), so their optimal corrections plausibly do too.
fastest_falsifying_experiment: Linearly interpolate two adapters trained at two corruption severities and test on the middle severity; endpoint-beating performance at the midpoint validates continuity in an afternoon.
core_claim: Trained adapters occupy a smooth low-dimensional manifold that a hypernetwork can parameterize, making generated adapters match stored ones and interpolations meaningful.
method_sketch: Train 10 domain adapters, fit a hypernetwork on 8, test reconstruction on 2 held-out; evaluate interpolated adapters on constructed intermediate-domain data (e.g., graded corruption levels).
novelty_hook: Hypernetworks for PEFT exist in NLP research; the manifold-continuity claim and intermediate-domain evaluation for segmentation appear new; unverified.
kill_risk: Held-out reconstruction may fail because 8 domains undersample the manifold, requiring an impractically large library.

title: Click policies versus weight adaptation at matched compute
one_line_idea: Train a small reinforcement-learned prompting policy that decides where to click next, and compare it head-to-head against LoRA adaptation for domain-shifted interactive segmentation at equal training compute.
problem: The community reflexively adapts weights when SAM underperforms, though smarter prompting might recover the same accuracy while keeping the model untouched and shareable.
core_hypothesis: For moderate shifts, a learned prompting policy operating on the frozen model matches LoRA's accuracy in the interactive setting, because failures are steerable rather than representational.
falsifiable_prediction: At matched training compute, policy-prompted frozen SAM reaches the same clicks-to-IoU frontier as LoRA-adapted SAM with naive prompting on moderate-shift datasets, and loses only on severe shifts.
why_important: Prompting policies are model-agnostic, instantly transferable across backbone versions, and deployable where weight modification is prohibited (regulated software).
why_possibly_novel: Interactive click policies predate SAM; the policy-vs-PEFT controlled comparison framing appears unexamined; unverified.
minimal_falsification_experiment: Train a click policy with simulated-oracle rewards on one shifted dataset; evaluate against LoRA under identical click simulators and compute accounting.
main_risk: RL training instability may consume the compute budget before a competent policy emerges, making the comparison unfair to policies.
community_default_belief: Weight adaptation is strictly more powerful than any prompting strategy on a frozen model.
why_it_might_be_wrong: The frozen model's reachable output set under optimal prompting has never been measured; it may cover far more of the target distribution than default prompting reveals.
fastest_falsifying_experiment: Estimate the oracle-prompt ceiling on a shifted dataset via exhaustive prompt search on a small sample; a ceiling below LoRA's known reach settles the question against policies immediately.
core_claim: For moderate shifts, a learned prompting policy operating on the frozen model matches LoRA's accuracy in the interactive setting, because failures are steerable rather than representational.
method_sketch: Train a click policy with simulated-oracle rewards on one shifted dataset; evaluate against LoRA under identical click simulators and compute accounting.
novelty_hook: Interactive click policies predate SAM; the policy-vs-PEFT controlled comparison framing appears unexamined; unverified.
kill_risk: RL training instability may consume the compute budget before a competent policy emerges, making the comparison unfair to policies.

title: Prompt-space test-time augmentation as a robustness layer
one_line_idea: Replace weight-space robustness training with test-time ensembling over systematically perturbed prompts, aggregating masks by pixel-wise voting into a robust prediction.
problem: Robustness for adapted SAM is pursued through training interventions, ignoring that promptable models expose a free ensemble axis at inference.
core_hypothesis: Prompt-jitter ensembling reduces error variance and boundary instability under distribution shift comparably to robustness-oriented fine-tuning, at zero training cost.
falsifiable_prediction: On corrupted or shifted test sets, 8-16 member prompt ensembles recover a substantial fraction of the robustness gap between a frozen model and a robustly fine-tuned one, especially on boundary metrics.
why_important: A training-free robustness layer stacks with any adapter and requires no data access, making it universally deployable.
why_possibly_novel: TTA over image transforms is standard; treating the prompt as the augmentation variable with a quantified robustness comparison seems fresh for segmentation; unverified.
minimal_falsification_experiment: Evaluate prompt-ensemble sizes and jitter magnitudes across clean and shifted datasets against single-prompt and image-TTA baselines, reporting accuracy and inference-cost curves.
main_risk: Ensembling may average away correct-but-minority mask hypotheses, hurting exactly the ambiguous cases it should help.
community_default_belief: Robustness must be trained in; inference-time tricks give marginal, unreliable gains.
why_it_might_be_wrong: The prompt dimension is an untapped source of independent errors, and ensemble gains scale with member independence—possibly more independent than image TTA transforms.
fastest_falsifying_experiment: Measure error decorrelation between masks from jittered prompts on one shifted dataset; high correlation across members means ensembling cannot help, ending the idea in hours.
core_claim: Prompt-jitter ensembling reduces error variance and boundary instability under distribution shift comparably to robustness-oriented fine-tuning, at zero training cost.
method_sketch: Evaluate prompt-ensemble sizes and jitter magnitudes across clean and shifted datasets against single-prompt and image-TTA baselines, reporting accuracy and inference-cost curves.
novelty_hook: TTA over image transforms is standard; treating the prompt as the augmentation variable with a quantified robustness comparison seems fresh for segmentation; unverified.
kill_risk: Ensembling may average away correct-but-minority mask hypotheses, hurting exactly the ambiguous cases it should help.

title: Weak heatmaps forged into prompts: WSSS through frozen SAM
one_line_idea: Train a tiny network that converts class-activation-style heatmaps from weak image-level labels into optimal SAM prompt sets, making frozen SAM the mask engine of weakly supervised segmentation.
problem: Weakly supervised segmentation pipelines refine noisy CAMs with hand-crafted heuristics, while a frozen promptable mask engine sits unused because nobody translates heatmaps into its prompt language properly.
core_hypothesis: A learned heatmap-to-prompt translator (choosing points, boxes, and negatives) extracts substantially better masks from frozen SAM than threshold-based prompt heuristics.
falsifiable_prediction: On standard weakly supervised protocols, the learned translator outperforms heuristic CAM-to-prompt conversion by a clear margin and approaches masks-from-full-supervision quality for well-localized classes.
why_important: Would upgrade the entire weak-supervision stack with zero segmentation labels, reframing WSSS as a prompt-translation problem.
why_possibly_novel: CAM-plus-SAM pipelines exist as heuristics; learning the translation end-to-end as the central object of study appears less explored; unverified.
minimal_falsification_experiment: Train the translator with only image-level labels using CAM inputs and mask-consistency rewards; evaluate against heuristic baselines on one standard WSSS benchmark setup.
main_risk: CAM localization errors may be the binding constraint, leaving little for better prompting to recover.
community_default_belief: The bottleneck in WSSS is localization quality of the weak signal, not how it is converted to masks.
why_it_might_be_wrong: SAM's mask prior is powerful enough that even crude localization plus well-chosen negatives may pin down the correct region, shifting the bottleneck to translation.
fastest_falsifying_experiment: Hand-optimize prompts from CAMs on 30 images and compare to heuristic conversion; if hand-optimal prompting barely helps, translation headroom is absent and the idea dies.
core_claim: A learned heatmap-to-prompt translator (choosing points, boxes, and negatives) extracts substantially better masks from frozen SAM than threshold-based prompt heuristics.
method_sketch: Train the translator with only image-level labels using CAM inputs and mask-consistency rewards; evaluate against heuristic baselines on one standard WSSS benchmark setup.
novelty_hook: CAM-plus-SAM pipelines exist as heuristics; learning the translation end-to-end as the central object of study appears less explored; unverified.
kill_risk: CAM localization errors may be the binding constraint, leaving little for better prompting to recover.

title: Information-optimal click placement, derived not guessed
one_line_idea: Derive click-placement rules that maximize expected information gain about the true mask under SAM's own posterior (multimask outputs plus scores), and train adapters under this principled interaction model.
problem: Click simulators used in training and evaluation place clicks by geometric heuristics (largest-error-region centers) with no theoretical grounding, potentially mis-training and mis-ranking interactive systems.
core_hypothesis: Clicks placed to maximally disambiguate SAM's mask hypotheses reduce clicks-to-target-IoU versus geometric heuristics, and adapters trained under the principled simulator transfer better to human clicking behavior.
falsifiable_prediction: Information-gain click selection dominates center-of-error heuristics on clicks-to-IoU curves across datasets, and simulator choice during training measurably changes adapter quality under human-behavior replay.
why_important: Interaction is half of the promptable-model system, currently governed by folklore; a normative theory would upgrade training, evaluation, and UI guidance simultaneously.
why_possibly_novel: Active perception theory is old; instantiating it over a promptable model's explicit hypothesis set for interactive segmentation appears new; unverified.
minimal_falsification_experiment: Implement the information-gain criterion over multimask hypotheses; compare simulators on frozen and adapted models; retrain adapters under each simulator and cross-evaluate.
main_risk: SAM's hypothesis set may be too impoverished (three masks) for information-gain computation to differ meaningfully from heuristics.
community_default_belief: Center-of-largest-error-region clicking is an adequate model of optimal and human interaction.
why_it_might_be_wrong: That heuristic ignores the model's actual uncertainty structure, which is precisely what determines the value of a click.
fastest_falsifying_experiment: On 50 images, compare one-step IoU improvement from information-gain vs heuristic clicks on the frozen model; indistinguishable means the richer criterion adds nothing at current hypothesis granularity.
core_claim: Clicks placed to maximally disambiguate SAM's mask hypotheses reduce clicks-to-target-IoU versus geometric heuristics, and adapters trained under the principled simulator transfer better to human clicking behavior.
method_sketch: Implement the information-gain criterion over multimask hypotheses; compare simulators on frozen and adapted models; retrain adapters under each simulator and cross-evaluate.
novelty_hook: Active perception theory is old; instantiating it over a promptable model's explicit hypothesis set for interactive segmentation appears new; unverified.
kill_risk: SAM's hypothesis set may be too impoverished (three masks) for information-gain computation to differ meaningfully from heuristics.

title: Learning where to look: domain-tuned everything-mode densities
one_line_idea: Adapt SAM's automatic mask generation to new domains by learning a spatial prompt-sampling density map instead of uniform grids, trained from unlabeled images via coverage objectives.
problem: Everything mode uses uniform grid prompts tuned for natural images, undersampling structures in domains where objects concentrate (tissue regions, crop rows) and wasting compute on empty space.
core_hypothesis: A learned domain-specific sampling density substantially improves proposal recall at fixed prompt budget compared to uniform grids, using only unlabeled target imagery.
falsifiable_prediction: At equal prompt counts, density-adapted everything mode raises instance recall meaningfully on domains with non-uniform object distributions and never falls below uniform sampling elsewhere.
why_important: Everything mode powers dataset bootstrapping and labeling tools; recall-per-compute improvements propagate through entire annotation economies.
why_possibly_novel: Prompt-grid tuning is treated as a fixed hyperparameter; learning it as a spatial policy per domain appears unstudied; unverified.
minimal_falsification_experiment: Learn density maps via self-supervised objectness cues on unlabeled data; evaluate proposal recall vs uniform and objectness-heuristic baselines at matched budgets on two domains.
main_risk: Recall gains may concentrate on easy structures, leaving the rare instances that matter unimproved.
community_default_belief: Uniform grid prompting is a neutral, adequate default for automatic mask generation.
why_it_might_be_wrong: Uniformity is only neutral under uniform object distributions—an assumption obviously false in most specialized domains.
fastest_falsifying_experiment: On one aerial dataset, reweight the grid by a simple saliency map and measure recall change at fixed budget; no improvement suggests density is not the binding constraint.
core_claim: A learned domain-specific sampling density substantially improves proposal recall at fixed prompt budget compared to uniform grids, using only unlabeled target imagery.
method_sketch: Learn density maps via self-supervised objectness cues on unlabeled data; evaluate proposal recall vs uniform and objectness-heuristic baselines at matched budgets on two domains.
novelty_hook: Prompt-grid tuning is treated as a fixed hyperparameter; learning it as a spatial policy per domain appears unstudied; unverified.
kill_risk: Recall gains may concentrate on easy structures, leaving the rare instances that matter unimproved.

title: A tiny bridge from text embeddings to SAM prompts
one_line_idea: Train only a small projection from a frozen text encoder's embeddings into SAM's prompt-token space, creating open-vocabulary text-prompted segmentation with both giants untouched.
problem: Text-promptable segmentation systems retrain heavy fusion modules, when the missing piece may be a low-dimensional alignment between two frozen embedding spaces.
core_hypothesis: A linear-or-tiny-MLP bridge suffices to steer SAM's decoder toward text-described objects for categories that are visually separable in SAM's feature space.
falsifiable_prediction: The bridge, trained on a modest set of region-text pairs, achieves meaningful referring-segmentation accuracy on held-out categories, with failures concentrated on categories SAM's features do not separate.
why_important: A parameter-tiny, frozen-backbone path to text-prompted segmentation would be the cheapest open-vocabulary mask system available, and diagnoses what SAM features already contain semantically.
why_possibly_novel: Text-to-SAM systems exist with substantial trained components; the minimal-bridge formulation as a scientific probe of embedding alignment seems distinct; unverified.
minimal_falsification_experiment: Train linear and 2-layer bridges on public region-text data; evaluate on held-out categories against chance and against full fusion architectures for context.
main_risk: SAM's prompt space may only encode geometry (where), not semantics (what), making text injection structurally impossible at this interface.
community_default_belief: Open-vocabulary segmentation requires deep vision-language fusion trained at scale.
why_it_might_be_wrong: The decoder already selects among competing objects using prompt tokens; if selection is semantic-capable, only a coordinate change may be missing.
fastest_falsifying_experiment: Optimize a per-category prompt token directly (no text) for 10 categories; if even direct optimization cannot make the decoder category-selective, the interface lacks the needed control and text-bridging is moot.
core_claim: A linear-or-tiny-MLP bridge suffices to steer SAM's decoder toward text-described objects for categories that are visually separable in SAM's feature space.
method_sketch: Train linear and 2-layer bridges on public region-text data; evaluate on held-out categories against chance and against full fusion architectures for context.
novelty_hook: Text-to-SAM systems exist with substantial trained components; the minimal-bridge formulation as a scientific probe of embedding alignment seems distinct; unverified.
kill_risk: SAM's prompt space may only encode geometry (where), not semantics (what), making text injection structurally impossible at this interface.

title: Self-correcting SAM: a learned second-round prompter
one_line_idea: Train a small module that inspects SAM's first mask and quality score, then emits corrective prompts for a second decoding pass, forming a two-round self-refinement loop with frozen weights.
problem: SAM's first answer is treated as final in automatic pipelines even though the model's own outputs contain signals (low scores, unstable regions) indicating correctable errors.
core_hypothesis: A learned critic-prompter recovers a meaningful share of first-pass errors by re-prompting, without any human input or weight adaptation.
falsifiable_prediction: Two-round self-correction improves mean IoU over single-pass output across shifted datasets, with gains concentrated on images whose first-pass quality score was low.
why_important: Turns SAM from a one-shot function into an introspective loop, a template applicable to any promptable model and free of retraining.
why_possibly_novel: Iterative refinement exists with humans in the loop; a learned autonomous re-prompter for promptable segmentation appears underexplored; unverified.
minimal_falsification_experiment: Train the prompter on one domain using first-pass errors as supervision; evaluate cross-domain two-round vs one-round performance and per-image gain vs first-pass score.
main_risk: Second-round prompts may help on the training domain but emit systematically harmful corrections under shift.
community_default_belief: Without new information (human clicks or labels), re-prompting cannot systematically improve outputs.
why_it_might_be_wrong: The first pass produces new information—the mask and its score—which conditions a smarter second query; the loop is not information-free.
fastest_falsifying_experiment: Oracle version: re-prompt using ground-truth-informed corrections on 50 images to measure the two-round ceiling; a low ceiling ends the project before training the critic.
core_claim: A learned critic-prompter recovers a meaningful share of first-pass errors by re-prompting, without any human input or weight adaptation.
method_sketch: Train the prompter on one domain using first-pass errors as supervision; evaluate cross-domain two-round vs one-round performance and per-image gain vs first-pass score.
novelty_hook: Iterative refinement exists with humans in the loop; a learned autonomous re-prompter for promptable segmentation appears underexplored; unverified.
kill_risk: Second-round prompts may help on the training domain but emit systematically harmful corrections under shift.

title: Prompt dropout makes adapters prompt-robust
one_line_idea: During adaptation, randomly degrade prompts (jitter, drop, wrong-type substitution) so adapters learn robustness to the sloppy prompting of real deployment.
problem: Adapters are trained with clean simulated prompts but deployed with imprecise human or upstream-model prompts, a mismatch that silently costs accuracy.
core_hypothesis: Prompt-degradation training trades a little clean-prompt accuracy for much larger robustness gains under realistic prompt noise, changing the deployed accuracy ranking of adapters.
